items.title: Iran, Qatar hold talks as Tehran weighs US diplomatic overture
items.description: Iranian and Qatari officials reportedly held talks over the weekend on proposals to end the conflict with the United States, as Tehran reviewed a US diplomatic overture but said it had no immediate plans for direct negotiations with Washington. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday that Tehran would decide whether to hold direct or indirect talks only after Washington agreed to its conditions. In an interview with Al Jazeera, Araghchi described a recent US effort to reopen dialogue as a positive step but dismissed reports of an imminent meeting between the two sides as speculation. Iranian negotiators met Qatari mediators in Doha on Saturday, following more than 12 hours of discussions between Iranian and Qatari envoys in Tehran on Friday, Reuters reported, citing a source. The talks were being coordinated through regular contacts with Washington. Araghchi said Iran's demands included the lifting of sanctions imposed after the Islamabad memorandum of understanding, the restoration of waivers for Iranian oil exports, the release of frozen Iranian assets and a reduction in US military forces in the region. Tehran also wanted an end to hostilities on all fronts, including Lebanon. On the Strait of Hormuz, Araghchi said Iran had reached agreement with mediators on a new proposal that could allow the waterway to be fully reopened within two days. Tehran also wants Washington to recognize a new shipping route developed with Oman, while other routes through the strait would be closed. The diplomatic efforts follow a letter from US Vice President JD Vance to Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, delivered through Qatari mediators. US media reports said the letter proposed direct negotiations led by Vance, with Iran's nuclear program on the agenda from the outset. Rezaei said the tone of the letter marked a significant shift in Washington's approach. He also said Iran was debating whether to abandon its longstanding ban on nuclear weapons if fighting resumed, although no decision had been made. The diplomatic contacts have done little to ease concerns about a return to fighting. Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned on Saturday that any new US or Israeli attack would be met with an immediate response without geographical restrictions. Iran's military later said it was taking steps to strengthen its readiness. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump had not decided whether to resume military action, adding that Washington preferred a diplomatic solution but was prepared to act if necessary. Trump, who launched the war alongside Israel on February 28, said on Friday that the conflict would end "very soon" but gave no details. Regional countries have been concerned that Washington could resume attacks after the US midterm elections. (Cover: A visitor to the Museum of Islamic Art takes pictures of the skyline of high-rise buildings in Doha on July 9, 2026. /VCG)

items.title: I am no more your leader, Wike is: Fubara faces uncertain future after surrendering
items.description: By Daniel Abia, P/Harcourt With dexterity and some sense of candor, he strode purposefully along the red carpet isle to the podium. His assigned role for the day was unambiguously defined: To unveil the Rainbow Coalition candidates for the 2027 general elections in Rivers State. But unknown to many, Governor Siminalayi Fubara had a special announcement to make. First, he took a brisk eye scan through the sea of heads at the Yakubu Gowon Stadium, then announced: “I am no more your leader. Stop calling me ‘my leader, my leader’” The day was Tuesday, October 27, 2026, when a political group formed by the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, FCT, Mr Nyesom Wike, organized a rally which drew participants from the 23 local government areas of the state. They converged on the Yakubu Gowon Stadium Port Harcourt to display which candidate from the six-member political parties that constitute the Rainbow Coalition for the coming elections. Fubara was tactically chosen to perform the unveiling and handover the flag of the All Progressives Congress, APC, to Hon Ogundu Kingsley Chinda, the anointed governorship candidate of Wike. Fubara did not only surrender his potential second term as a sitting governor to Chinda but also relinquished his role as the political leader of Rivers to Wike. The governor veered off the track of duty and handed down a stern warning, or so it seemed, to his organic supporters who stood by him in thick and thin during the dark moment of the political crisis in Rivers, telling them unreservedly that he was no more their leader. “Let me say something here so that it will always help us while we move forward”, he started. “I’m aware there are some issues where some persons who followed me when we had the crisis when you’re in your meeting you say ‘my leader, my leader’. “We are now in one house. And because we have one house, there is no issue about who is the leader. “I might be your oga (governor) but we have a common leader now. So, please, going forward, this issue of ‘my leader, my leader, my leader’, I want it resolved here and now.” There was a cumulus of silence at first, then a deafening applause. Governors as leaders Way back in January 2025, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, through his Vice, Kasim Shettima, had declared that all APC governors were political leaders of the party in their states. The implication is that as the highest political position in the state, a governor is seen as a leader politically. Tinubu made this known during the defection of Governor Agbu Kefas of Taraba State from PDP to APC. That pronouncement also covered Fubara the moment he defected from the same PDP to APC on December 9, 2025 and picked the 001 registration number of the ruling party. Also, shortly after Fubara’s defection, APC national leaders—including National Chairman, Prof Nentawe Yilwatda, National Secretary, Ajibola Basiru, and Deputy National Organising Secretary, Duru Eze, officially affirmed the Rivers governor as the leader of the APC in the state. They cited the APC Constitution, which designates sitting state governors as party leaders in their respective states. Rainbow/Fubara reconciliation Reeling in the deep cut injury occasioned by the over three years of political crisis that culminated into the declaration of a state of emergency on March 18, 2025 by President Tinubu, Wike and his political group soon realized the need to bring in Fubara and his structure to form a formidable force for 2027. Between August 16 and October 7, 2026, the Rainbow Coalition led by Wike held a back-to-back peace meeting with the governor in his private residence in Port Harcourt. The last meeting, expanded to include all the 23 LGA chairmen, had lawmakers from both state and national assemblies and political appointees loyal to Wike in attendance. At the meeting, Fubara accepted to return to the “family”. And the three suspended lawmakers loyal to him were reinstated while members of his political camp were promised juicy positions in the next dispensation. The peace meeting generated outrage in Rivers with many describing the governor as the “weakest” political leader in the history of Rivers. Fubara was alleged to have told his loyalists to go to the rural areas across the state and preach the gospel of Rainbow Coalition. State capture? Political observers are of the opinion that, having used his structure to propel Fubara to become governor, Wike was making a grand plan to capture the soul of the state. The internecine crisis witnessed in the past, obviously testified to the fact that the minister “was desperate for a third term by proxy”, said Franklin Uket, a public commentator. Uket noted that from the fight to regain his structure, “Wike never wanted Fubara to be independent minded as a governor. “He never wanted Fubara to draw any of his (Wike) political enemies close to his government”. Now politically suffocated, Fubara’s decision to throw in the towel of leadership also gives credence to the fact that the crisis is deeper than what appears in the surface. “The governor has been stampeded and bullied out of power”, Uket alleged. Public perception Apparently miffed by the recent development, Fubara’s former ally and royal father, HRH Ubokikwan Gabriel Ogbologwung, PhD, Paramount Ruler of Egwebe in Andoni LGA of the state, said “the summersault position taken by the Executive Governor of Rivers State, Siminalayi Joseph Fubara, in my thinking is not an excellent decision”. The monarch said Fubara’s statement gives credence to what many see as using the governor “as a tool for the state’s total capture placing the state under Minister Nyesom Wike’s political egoistic jackboot” He said the governor’s latest move has made most of his followers, especially as the grassroots, to shrink back into their political shells. “With Fubara’s ignominious move, he has totally surrendered his political life for a terminal crush by Nyesom Wike, who left nothing for Governor Fubara on the negation tables, which architect -in-chief is Wike and Wike alone”. Ogbologwung said as a Rivers man, “I see the governor’s total surrender to Wike as a ship captain who swims ashore with the only life-buoy available during a wreck without bothering about the safety of his crew members. “The governor’s action has sadly demonstrated to the world how not to have a leader with a borrowed mind. “As a result, he has, by his own inconsiderate machinations deliberately sunk his political ship, having eaten to his own belle-full, that he desires less of neither the survival of his followers nor the state itself”. Another supporter of the governor and an elder statesman of Ijaw extraction, Chief Anabs Sara-Igbe, reiterated that Rivers people are not in sync with Wike’s political posturing. He said Fubara must have been forced to relinquish his leadership role because “he has found himself in a web”. Sara-Igbe said the governor’s action may have serious future implication on political balance of the state. “What he did may have a deeper meaning. Wike has been begging Fubara since, it means that he wanted to take total power from Fubara. But we are waiting”. Speaking differently, a former member of the House of Representatives and a political analyst, Prince Ogbonna Nwuke, said the governor’s action could be deduced from the context of how he sees himself presently. “There is nothing too big for anybody to do to bring peace. You can’t have two masters in the same boat”, Ogbonna said, adding that only Fubara can answer why he voluntarily surrender his leadership to Wike. The former commissioner however stated that as things stand now, “Fubara has taken a backstage in the state politics. I don’t know if I should say it is humility or weakness. But the governor is not ego-driven or power-drunk”. According to him, the governor’s supporters must have felt let down, disappointed and shocked. “He may have plans for his people on what to do for them to ameliorate the pains of what has just happened”, Ogbonna concluded. For the President of the pan Niger Delta Elders Forum, PANDEF, Prof (Amb) Godknows Igali, there was nothing strange about what Fubara did. “He is entitled to his opinion or action. In the beginning, they were in the same political family”, Igali said. The diplomat said that interest, in whatever form or shape, is determined by whoever is the political leader of the state. “It is Fubara’s right to relinquish authority or to hold onto it”, he said. Implication Governor Fubara may not envisage any further political power again after his tenure. But the question many are asking is: What possible impact will that action have on the people of Opobo, his ancestral home! Will they be trusted with political in the nearest future! More so, what is the assurance that Fubara and his team are in the Rainbow Coalition camp with their full chest! The answers are in the belle of the 2027 governorship election in the state. But for now, he is on hangar’s cliff. The post I am no more your leader, Wike is: Fubara faces uncertain future after surrendering appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: 77 days to polls:Parties clash over INEC’s preparations
items.description: By Henry Umoru, Luminous Jannamike & Omeiza Ajayi With barely 77 days to the 2027 general elections, concerns over the preparedness of the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, have become disturbing, especially following the discovery of artificial intelligence-generated photographs in the commission’s preliminary voters’ register. The development has raised fresh questions about the integrity of the electoral database, the effectiveness of INEC’s internal monitoring mechanisms and the commission’s capacity to conduct elections that would command public confidence. Accordingly, the worries have been compounded by complaints about other irregularities in the preliminary register, including questionable names, addresses, genders and photographs. Although INEC has acknowledged the problem and promised to clean up the register before the final version is released on December 15, 2026, the development has exposed vulnerabilities in the registration process. The commission’s Director of Information and Communication Technology, ICT, Dr Lawrence Bayode, disclosed that some registration officers allegedly used their official login credentials to introduce irregular entries into the database. He, however, assured Nigerians that the commission had identified those responsible and was taking steps to address the situation. Registered voters INEC’s preliminary register, uploaded on October 26, 2026, contains over 103.4 million registered voters. Bayode explained that the figure reflected the more than 93 million voters recorded in the 2023 register and additional registrations from the continuous voter registration exercise ahead of the forthcoming elections. He said INEC was deploying technology to address the identified shortcomings, adding that its Automated Biometric Identification System, ABIS, had detected several questionable photographs before the preliminary register was released. Against this backdrop, Sunday Vanguard spoke with officials of political parties to ascertain their assessment of INEC’s preparations, the implications of the AI-generated images and what the commission needs to do to guarantee credible elections. While some parties expressed reservations about the development and called for urgent measures to restore public confidence, others maintained that the discovery should not be exaggerated, insisting that INEC had sufficient time to address the identified problems. LP: INEC must go back to drawing board For the Labour Party, LP, the discovery of AI-generated photographs in the preliminary voters’ register is a development that requires urgent attention, particularly given the proximity of the elections. The party’s National Publicity Secretary, Ken Asogwa, said the situation had moved beyond speculation following the commission’s admission that irregularities had occurred. He said: “This is quite concerning. This is no longer a rumour because even INEC Director of ICT came out to admit it.” Asogwa expressed concern that such a development was occurring under the leadership of the current INEC Chairman, Prof. Joash Ojo Amupitan, SAN, whom he described as a person with considerable academic and professional credentials. He said: “This is happening at a time when we have an INEC Chairman who is not just a lawyer, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria at that. If you look at his CV, he is also an academic of repute, an individual who was a Deputy Vice Chancellor of a University.” According to him, the proximity of the elections makes the development particularly disturbing. “That this is happening with less than 90 days to a crucial election is worrisome,” he added. On the commission’s preparedness, the LP spokesman said INEC was in the best position to assess and explain its readiness. However, he insisted that the commission had a responsibility to reassure Nigerians and rebuild confidence in the electoral process. He said: “As to their preparedness, the commission is in the best place to say. But we will suggest that they go back to the drawing board and inspire public confidence in the process. “Election also has a lot to do with public perception.” PDP: No cause for alarm However, the Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, adopted a different position, expressing confidence in the commission’s activities and urging political parties and other stakeholders not to make the discovery appear bigger than it is. The party’s National Publicity Secretary, Jungudo Haruna Mohammed, acknowledged that complaints had emerged from different quarters over the preliminary voters’ register, particularly allegations involving AI-generated images. He, however, said INEC’s admission and commitment to correcting the anomalies should be acknowledged. He said: “We have received complaints from different quarters, particularly about the preliminary voters’ register, where it was alleged that AI-generated images had been included. It is no longer an allegation because INEC has owned up to it. “The good thing is that INEC has acknowledged the issue and reassured Nigerians that it is doing everything possible to correct it and prevent a recurrence.” AI-generated Mohammed argued that the emergence of AI-generated images in the register was not entirely surprising, considering the growing influence of artificial intelligence in contemporary society. He, however, maintained that the discovery did not necessarily suggest that the electoral process had been compromised. “In today’s world, where AI has become the order of the day, it is not surprising that such images may have found their way into the register. However, now that the issue has been discovered, I do not think it has the potential to discredit the credibility of the electoral process. “Whatever number of AI-generated images of purported eligible voters may have infiltrated the register is unlikely to be significant enough to affect the outcome of the elections.” The PDP spokesman further noted that the register currently in circulation was preliminary and not the final document to be used for the elections. According to him, the commission still has the opportunity to identify and eliminate questionable entries before the final register is published. “The good thing is that this is not the final register, and these issues have been detected very early. We believe INEC will deploy all necessary technologies to clean up the register and prevent it from being infiltrated by questionable and unverifiable entries,” he said. On the general preparedness of the commission, Mohammed said his party had not identified anything that suggested that the forthcoming elections were under threat. “For our party, we have not seen anything so far that has the capacity to truncate the 2027 elections. I think INEC’s preparations so far deserve a level of commendation. “The commission has outlined about 14 or 15 items it intends to achieve, and from the last information I received from the INEC chairman, it has achieved about 10 of them. “Our party is therefore not worried. We are making our own preparations, and so far, INEC’s activities have not given us any cause for concern.” Electoral process He also called on opposition parties and public commentators to be measured in their public statements, warning against utterances that could undermine confidence in the electoral process. “I will call on opposition parties and public commentators to guard their utterances. “We need the country. We need a peaceful country. We need to encourage INEC, and I must also commend Nigerians for being very vigilant. “This shows that the level of civic responsibility among Nigerians has risen. In the past, Nigerians did not really pay much attention to the voters’ register. But now, they are clearly watching, observing every step and scrutinising everything INEC does.” Mohammed said the growing public scrutiny should encourage the commission to remain committed to transparency. “Overall, INEC is now aware that Nigerians are very vigilant. The commission, on its part, will not contemplate doing anything that could truncate or compromise the electoral process. “The PDP is confident in INEC’s activities, and we believe the concerns that have been raised are minor issues. INEC owned up to them, which is commendable. “If it had denied the issue, that would have given us reason to doubt. But it did not. It acknowledged that it had identified the problem and was cleaning up the register. “We must all rally support behind INEC, commend the Commission and remain positive about the 2027 elections and transition,” he added. APM: AI must not undermine credible elections On its part, the Allied People’s Movement, APM, expressed concerns about the application of artificial intelligence in the electoral process, stressing the need for caution and responsible deployment of the technology. The party’s National Publicity Secretary, Abubakar Yusuf, said INEC must remain alive to its responsibilities, particularly as the country approaches another crucial electoral exercise. According to him, the commission must ensure that the introduction of technology does not defeat the fundamental objective of conducting credible elections. He said: “INEC is expected to be alive to its responsibilities, particularly when it comes to elections at any level. “On the issue of artificial intelligence, the need for caution and its responsible deployment is obvious. This is necessary to ensure that the objectives of using the technology are not defeated.” Yusuf insisted that the 2027 elections must be conducted in a manner that leaves no room for questions about their credibility, acceptability and verifiability. He said:“The 2027 polls must be seen to be acceptable, credible and verifiable in every respect. Anything short of that will raise questions about INEC’s conduct of the elections. “The deployment of AI should not undermine the genuine objective of ensuring credible polls.” For the APM, therefore, the controversy surrounding the preliminary register reinforces the need for INEC to exercise greater vigilance in deploying technology and managing the electoral database. SDP: INEC is compromised Taking the same position, the Adewole Adebayo-Bugaje Presidential Campaign Council of the Social Democratic Party, SDP, faulted INEC’s preparations in view of prevailing issues. The council said the current level of preparation was fundamentally compromised, characterised by severe vulnerabilities in technological integrity and institutional transparency, just 77 days before citizens head to the polls. Speaking to Sunday Vanguard in Abuja, the campaign council’s Chief Media and Communications Adviser, Comrade Mark Adebayo, said while Prof. Joash Amupitan-led INEC continued to offer verbal assurances of its readiness, the SDP’s empirical analysis of the National Voters’ Register, biometric infrastructure deployment and logistical timelines revealed systemic red flags that threatened the credibility of the upcoming elections. Vulnerabilities Adebayo said: “Our campaign maintains that the Independent National Electoral Commission’s (INEC) current level of preparation is fundamentally compromised, characterised by severe vulnerabilities in technological integrity and institutional transparency just 80 days before citizens head to the polls. While INEC continues to offer verbal assurances of its readiness, our empirical analysis of the National Voters’ Register, biometric infrastructure deployment, and logistical timelines reveals systemic red flags that threaten the credibility of the upcoming elections. “We refuse to allow structural defects to be swept under the rug. We seriously suspect that distinct algorithmic anomalies consistent with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) may have been deployed and active on INEC platforms. These are not human voters; they are synthetic identities designed to pad the register. “Statistical analysis reveals an improbable statistical spike in registered voters aged 18-22 in specific strategic clusters, where the registration curve completely diverges from historical census data and local birth rates. “INEC’s Automated Biometric Identification System (ABIS) was legally mandated to eliminate duplicates and non-human data. The presence of these glaring AI fabrications is empirical proof that either the ABIS software is malfunctioning, or it has been deliberately bypassed. “Beyond the compromised register, our active tracking of INEC’s field readiness indicates a dangerous lag in critical operational benchmarks. BVAS auditing “On the limited mock trials, field reports show unrectified battery degradation and software latency in rural local governments. We explicitly demand electoral integrity. “We will not sit idly by while the democratic will of the people is subverted by technological malpractice. On behalf of our candidate, Prince Adewole Adebayo, and millions of hopeful citizens, we demand that INEC immediately execute the following corrective measures: “Independent Digital Audit: INEC must grant accredited joint-party IT experts and independent international observers direct read-only access to the central backend register to conduct a comprehensive algorithmic sweep for AI-generated faces. “Transparent BVAS Auditing: A public, televised stress-test of the BVAS machines across all senatorial districts must be conducted within the next 14 days to verify biometric match speeds and battery resilience. “Purging of the Register: A comprehensive, publicly verifiable list of all deleted, duplicated, or flagged synthetic entries must be published by polling unit, ensuring absolute mathematical reconciliation before final printing. “Let us be clear, our campaign wants an election, but we insist on a legitimate election. We are not asking for favours; we are demanding compliance with the law and technological accountability. INEC has exactly 80 days to cleanse its systems, secure its portals, and prove to the world that it is an umpire, not an accomplice. The resilience of our democracy depends entirely on their next move.” Preparations Also speaking with Sunday Vanguard on the development, the National Chairman of the Action Democratic Party, ADP, Yabagi Yusuf Sani, said that with elections barely 80 days away, INEC must demonstrate its preparedness through verifiable actions, not mere assurances. The ADP has called for an immediate, transparent and independent investigation into the irregularities, identification of those responsible, appropriate sanctions where wrongdoing is established, and a comprehensive forensic audit of the voters’ register before its final certification. Sani said: “The position of the Action Democratic Party (ADP) is that the credibility of any election begins long before polling day. It starts with the integrity of the voters’ register, the transparency of electoral preparations, the neutrality of electoral officials and the confidence of Nigerians in the entire electoral process. “The recent revelations concerning alleged AI-generated photographs and other irregularities in the voters’ register are deeply concerning. The reported acknowledgement by INEC’s Director of ICT that some registration officers introduced AI-generated photographs into the system raises serious questions about the effectiveness of the Commission’s internal controls and safeguards against electoral manipulation. Investigation “ADP therefore calls for an immediate, transparent and independent investigation into these irregularities, identification of those responsible, appropriate sanctions where wrongdoing is established, and a comprehensive forensic audit of the voters’ register before its final certification. “With elections barely 80 days away, INEC must demonstrate its preparedness through verifiable actions rather than mere assurances. Nigerians deserve clear evidence that the voters’ register is credible, electoral technologies are reliable, sensitive materials are secure, and arrangements for voting, collation and transmission of results are sufficiently robust to prevent manipulation. “We are particularly concerned that technological innovations intended to strengthen electoral credibility could become instruments for undermining public confidence if adequate safeguards, transparency and accountability are lacking. “INEC must also deepen its engagement with political parties, civil society organisations, security agencies and other stakeholders. The Commission must address outstanding concerns arising from previous elections and demonstrate measurable improvements in its operational readiness. “For ADP, the fundamental issue is not simply whether INEC can conduct elections on schedule, but whether every eligible Nigerian can exercise the right to vote freely and whether every lawful vote will be accurately counted, transparently collated and faithfully reflected in the declared results. “Nigeria cannot afford another electoral process overshadowed by avoidable controversies, technological uncertainties and allegations of manipulation. “Our message to INEC is clear: electoral credibility must be demonstrated, not merely proclaimed. “The integrity of the 2027 elections is too important to be compromised by administrative lapses, technological vulnerabilities or institutional complacency.” NDC: Remove names of deceased Nigerians Reacting to the development, the National Presidential Campaign Council, NPCC, of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, urged INEC to remove the names of deceased Nigerians from the voters’ register. According to the NDC, reports that deceased Nigerians still appear on the voters’ register raise serious questions about its accuracy and integrity. A statement by the spokesperson for the NPCC of the NDC, Dr Chiogo Constance Ikokwu, called on the electorate and political parties to take advantage of their rights and file objections with the electoral body so that INEC could effect the removals. The statement reads: “Reports that deceased Nigerians, including prominent figures such as Raymond Dokpesi, Ifeanyi Ubah, Muhammadu Buhari and Rotimi Akeredolu, still appear on the voters’ register raise serious questions about its accuracy and integrity. “These are just a few names. What about the 774 local government areas across Nigeria? How many deceased persons remain on the register? When was it last comprehensively updated? Is this an oversight, institutional failure or something more troubling? Citizens “INEC has the legal responsibility to cleanse the register, especially if it has been notified by citizens. The electoral body owes Nigerians answers. We demand a credible, up-to-date and verifiable voters’ register ahead of the 2027 elections. “We call on Nigerians and political parties to take advantage of their rights and file objections to the electoral body so INEC can effect removals. On its part, INEC needs to look into these complaints, establish a portal to put all names under objection and give persons against whom a complaint has been lodged the opportunity to respond (in the case of the living), as well as publishing the procedure to object to illegal names in the interest of the public. The electoral body is a well-funded organisation paid for by citizens, and therefore must provide value for money. “Nigerians will accept nothing less than the highest standards of efficiency, professionalism and accountability from INEC. The electoral body must demonstrate that it has the capacity, competence and commitment to deliver an election whose credibility cannot reasonably be called into question. This is not too much to ask; it is the bare minimum expected of an institution entrusted with the people’s democratic mandate. “Furthermore, in light of the 2023 election credibility challenges, it is time for an independent, unbiased and professional audit of INEC processes and mechanisms. The 2027 election is too critical for unanswered questions about the very foundation of our democracy. No excuses. No complacency. No questionable register. INEC must do its job.” 4,800 claims, 600 objections Meanwhile, INEC said it had received over 4,800 claims and about 600 objections to the preliminary voters’ register, with a promise that the discrepancies would be corrected before the final register was certified on December 15, 2026. INEC Chairman, Professor Joash Amupitan, SAN, disclosed this on Friday when the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) Pre-Election Fact-Finding Mission paid a courtesy visit to the commission’s headquarters in Abuja. The mission is led by Victor Bockarie Foh, a former Vice-President of Sierra Leone. Amupitan said the claims, received at the registration areas where the register was displayed as of Thursday, were mainly corrections and other minor matters. On objections, he said the commission had received “about 600 complaints on the register” through electoral officers and Resident Electoral Commissioners from the various wards. He added that “the display of the register online is also confirming some of the complaints we had earlier received.” According to him, the register now stands at over 103 million registered citizens, adding that it is a huge figure and that the discrepancies noticed would be corrected so that “the register will be properly cleaned up” ahead of the final list. 8,809 Registration Areas The commission completed three phases of the Continuous Voter Registration exercise and recently ended the physical display of the preliminary register at registration areas nationwide. It has also published the register on its online portal, display.inecnigeria.org , for public scrutiny, claims and objections. He again restated that the Presidential and National Assembly elections will hold on Saturday, January 16, 2027, while the Governorship and State Houses of Assembly elections are scheduled for Saturday, February 6, 2027. He said the commission will deploy personnel and technology across 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, covering 774 Local Government Areas, 8,809 Registration Areas (Wards) and 176,846 polling units. Amupitan said the commission had executed nine of the 14 major milestones in its Revised Timetable and Schedule of Activities for the election. He said INEC had also moved “away from administrative assumptions” by personally conducting zonal readiness assessment tours. It has covered the South-West in Lagos, the North-West in Kaduna, the South-East in Enugu and the North-East in Gombe, and the team is heading to Port Harcourt for the South-South. The North-Central, the last zone, will be visited next week. Accreditation He said the tours had shown that some areas needed higher deployments than planned because of terrain and security challenges. Amupitan disclosed that the commission was planning a mock accreditation across the country, which he said should hold “sometime in November.” He said it would test accreditation and the transmission of results simultaneously in all the states, to be sure the commission can “cure the problem of glitch that took place in 2023.” On technology, he said the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) would be deployed for dual biometric accreditation, by fingerprint and face. The commission has also introduced a new electronic verification platform, eEC8A, for results transmitted to the INEC Result Viewing Portal (IReV). Electoral integrity However, beyond the positions of the parties, the controversy has placed renewed attention on the responsibility of INEC to demonstrate that the problems identified in the preliminary register are being addressed. Observers believe the commission’s December 15 deadline for the release of the final register will, therefore, be an important test of its ability to resolve the concerns raised by stakeholders. INEC, therefore, faces the task of convincing Nigerians that the preliminary register’s shortcomings will not translate into weaknesses in the final electoral process. The post 77 days to polls:Parties clash over INEC’s preparations appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Fasoranti’s death: Rumbling in Yorubaland, a new Afenifere may emerge
items.description: Old guard moves to form ‘Afenifere Independent’ Oba Olaitan calls for truce Forceful acquisition of pan-Yoruba group is dead on arrival —Ex-spokesman ‘Without Adebanjo’s camp support for Peter Obi, Tinubu may not have been president’ By Dapo Akinrefon The leadership crisis within the pan-Yoruba socio-political organization, Afenifere, may be far from being over. This is as a result of a factional camp asking other factions to unite behind the leadership of Oba Oladipo Olaitan. But while most of the Fasoranti camp vowed to resist such a move, some of the old guards, it was gathered, plan to form another Afenifere. Most of them, who belong to various factions, disagree over cultural succession norms and the potential emergence of a break-away Yoruba group. A source told Sunday Vanguard that discussions are ongoing to jettison both camps and start on a clean slate. Multiple sources said there is a need to resuscitate Afenifere and give the Yoruba race a formidable platform. A credible source informed Vanguard that while some members of the group are making moves to throw up what they called Afenifere Independent, the Akure camp is gearing up to name a former governor as Fasoranti’s successor. The source said: “One thing I know is that the Akure camp will not approve that Oba Oladipo Olaitan emerges as Afenifere leader. I know who they are planning to name as Fasoranti’s successor. He is a former governor. The two camps cannot be united as it is and that is why some of us having made up our mind to come up with Afenifere Independent.” Last week, following the death of Pa Reuben Fasoranti, the Oba Olaitan camp formally announced the consolidation of its collective leadership under his (Olaitan’s) stewardship. It said the transition was a tribute to Fasoranti’s legacy and a step towards promoting unity and defending Yoruba socio-political interests. The factional National Publicity Secretary and Secretary-General, Prince Justice Faloye and Alade Rotimi-John respectively, said Olaitan had demonstrated sincerity of purpose and the capacity to champion the group’s interests while promoting national unity. The statement read: “The modern history of the Yoruba people and the political evolution of Nigeria bear the indelible mark of Fasoranti. As a patriarch of principles, Pa Fasoranti carried the sacred torch of Afenifere with unyielding grace, following in the visionary footsteps of Chief Obafemi Awolowo, Chief Adekunle Ajasin and Senator Abraham Adesanya. Through seasons of national uncertainty, he stood as a steadfast moral compass, a relentless advocate for true federalism, equity, fairness and the progressive advancement of his people. His leadership anchored the Yoruba nation in wisdom, courage and an unshakeable commitment to justice and fair play.” In their defence, they were of the view that the consolidation of the great legacy now rests upon Oba Oladipo Olaitan, while they insisted that the time for division is over. The statement further said: “Over the years, Oba Olaitan has demonstrated a profound sincerity of purpose and the strategic capacity to champion the core interests of Afenifere while simultaneously promoting the greater unity of Nigeria. His track record reflects a leader who understands the delicate balance between popular advocacy within a region and the broader imperative of national cohesion. Afenifere hereby issues a solemn clarion call to all factions, political actors and upcoming generations within the Yoruba nation that the time for division is over. The survival, stability and prosperity of the Yoruba people now depend on absolute pan-Yoruba unity. We urge all sons and daughters of Omo kaaro oojiire to close ranks, eschew the politics of bitterness and hatred, and unite firmly behind the leadership of Oba Olaitan. Together, we look towards a future in which historical injustices will be rectified and Yoruba heritage and interests secured in a fair and equitable society under God. In assuming this sacred mandate, Oba Olaitan is entrusted with the responsibility of leading with an absolute sense of purpose and unassailable dignity. As a traditional ruler, he is steeped in the exercise of restraint, the application of wisdom and the dignified statesmanship assured by his royal pedigree. He knows how to remain immune to transient political persuasions and undue pressures, holding his leadership position not as a political office but as a divine trust for the collective protection of our institutions and people.” The statement drew the ire of some Afenifere chieftains who expressed disappointment over the faction’s position. Following the backlash of the statement, Oba Olaitan, Sunday Vanguard gathered, had called for a meeting. This reporter was informed that Oba Olaitan had seen the handwriting on the wall that his leadership may not go down well even within his camp, hence the need for a meeting on Thursday. It’s premature to discuss succession plan —Falae The Chairman of the National Executive Committee of Afenifere, Oba Olu Falae, distanced himself from the Olaitan camp’s stand, saying the move was premature. Falae also said it was contrary to Yoruba culture to discuss leadership succession before the burial of its late leader, Pa Reuben Fasoranti. Oba Falae, who spoke in Akure when a condolence message was delivered to the family, had said it was inappropriate to discuss who succeeds a leader before he is buried. Taking a swipe at the Olaitan camp, the former Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF) insisted that the priority of the organization is to give Pa Fasoranti a befitting burial, after which a credible leader would emerge to lead the group. He had said: “Any discussion on leadership succession is premature and contrary to Yoruba culture. It is inappropriate to discuss who succeeds a leader before he is buried.” Forceful acquisition of Afenifere is dead on arrival —Adejumo Shedding light on the controversy surrounding Afenifere, a former spokesperson for the Yoruba body, Mogaji Gboyega Adejumo—an Afenifere Independent—spoke on the ideological divide and question of leadership. He also emphasised that Yoruba politics has been divided since the era of Chief Obafemi Awolowo. Awolowo championed egalitarianism, democratic socialism, and ethical civic responsibility (Omoluabi). Adejumo said: “How does someone simply wake up one day and announce himself as the leader in a situation where two distinct and ideologically different factions exist?” Going down memory lane, the Afenifere chieftain explained the Yoruba concept of Omoluabi, which he said has shaped Yoruba politics for decades. His words: “Ever since Chief Obafemi Awolowo entered Yoruba politics, and perhaps Nigerian politics more broadly, two distinct tendencies have existed side by side. On the one hand is the progressivism Awolowo introduced which, in some ways, reflects the Yoruba concept of Omoluabi, although it goes much further. This ideological divide has shaped Yoruba politics for decades. Consider everything Awolowo accomplished: His many firsts, his exemplary personal life and integrity, and what he achieved in just nine years in office. Reproducing that record would be extraordinarily difficult because of his commitment to ethics, civic responsibility, social development, and a clear pathway to success across different sectors. His achievements included Africa’s first television station, a modern secretariat, a modern stadium, and the development of Government Reserved Areas such as Bodija and Ikeja GRA. He also helped attract industries and businesses through the philosophy of democratic socialism. Yet reactionary tendencies have persisted throughout Yorubaland among people who present themselves as progressives. Given enough time, those tendencies often reveal themselves. These forces gained the upper hand during the 1962 crisis, when some Yoruba political actors chose to align themselves with the North. We associate that tendency with feudalism and entrenched corruption. Some Yoruba people simply did not appreciate the Spartan lifestyle Awolowo practised and expected others in public life to embrace. Awolowo wanted a society founded on the principle of the idea that people should be treated with equal dignity, regardless of their background. His vision was one of egalitarianism, fairness, equal opportunity, and justice. But the reactionaries prevailed, contributing to the 1962 crisis, the ensuing counter-accusations, and a series of political irregularities. Today, we have development commissions across Nigeria’s six geopolitical zones. Yet Awolowo had already demonstrated the importance of institutionalised development through the Western Region’s development initiatives, particularly the Western Nigeria Development Corporation (WNDC). Awolowo’s ideas were far ahead of those of his reactionary opponents. But the reactionaries had an advantage: They understood the appeal of local loyalties and used it to draw people to their side. The crisis ultimately contributed to Awolowo’s prosecution on charges of treasonable felony, which he maintained were trumped up, and his imprisonment. Other members of his political circle, including S. G. Ikoku and Ayo Adebanjo, also faced persecution. Following the overthrow of Kwame Nkrumah in Ghana, where they had sought refuge, they were deported to Nigeria and served prison terms. There is something we may never forget, Awolowo never meant for Afenifere to be a Yoruba irredentist group and that should be something that should guide anyone who wants to be the leader. In one of Papa Awolowo’s book, he almost placed a curse on anyone who wants to turn Afenifere into a Yoruba irredentist group. Awolowo maintained that till the end of his life and charged all members to look at Afenifere as a national party. The reason we are Afenifere is because Chief Akinloye gave us that name in 1951 so as to express the meaning of ‘life more abundant’ to the people at the grassroots. If Nigeria must progress, the feudal system in the North must die and Awolowo has said that many times. He maintained it to the end and charged all members that any part of the country that is not aligned with this philosophy, we must go there and plant it, so that we can all begin to see a country that is devoid of feudalism and other forms of cultural interferences that are anti civilisation. Take for example, if Awolowo was not right, how come Afenifere was leader of the opposition in the East when S.G Ikokwu of the Action Group defeated his father, Alvan Ikokwu, of the NCNC. Afenifere later became the leader of the opposition winning at least six seats in the Eastern region. In the North, Afenifere became the leader of opposition with Alhaji Maito of the Action Group and we had about eight members. No other party succeeded in having that. Northern People Congress (NPC) did not have a single seat in any of the places to form the opposition leader. Only the NCNC was able to do that in the West. That is the philosophy written down in plain sight that Pa Adebanjo followed. Awolowo would cry in his grave to know that a leader, chosen after him, playing the Yoruba irredentist politics that will make it look like Afenifere is only for the Yoruba. That is the bastardization of the Awolowo philosophy. It was only Adebanjo that followed it to the last. The successor of Adebanjo, who is the present Chairman of the SMBLF, has already thrown Adebanjo under the bus. It would lead us to know that the adage of Uthman Dan Fodio which he said that do not trust any man that goes into his household to steal their valuables to give a stranger because such a man will not hesitate to give yours away to other suitors. Forceful acquisition is dead on arrival. So, if someone is trying to throw Adebanjo and those who believe in him under the bus and is tracing his predecessors (Fasoranti, Adesanya, Ajasin and Awolowo) and painfully excluded Adebanjo, then, it is never going to be easy. We are going to have a serious crisis. The Akure people, I have certain feelings and have been getting certain feelers that they will not go along with this. They have formidable people. The Yoruba are not going to be forcefully taken by anyone, it is not going to happen. Let us be clear that this forceful acquisition is dead on arrival.” Forming a third force in Afenifere Adejumo continued: “My final contribution to this development would be a concerning call I received from one of our respected elders in the Afenifere, Dr Femi Okurounmu, about three weeks ago and said to me that the two factions of Afenifere are on their death rows. It is almost as if life has departed from Afenifere. He said ‘I and some others have decided to form a third force.’ I promptly rejected that idea because my position is that we have a greater danger ahead of us in the forthcoming elections. The people may not be readily open to having another group because the focus now is the January presidential election. I said ‘why don’t we wait till after the elections and see how we can fit in, where leadership should go and see how we can return Afenifere back to factory mode. Enough of the usurpers and pretenders’. That is what I told him not knowing that a lot of these things will begin to unfold to lend credence to my position that nothing should be done for now. In the tradition of the Yoruba, when a leader dies, nobody talks about succession until that leader has been given a befitting burial. Then, of course, we cannot be having all these controversial tendencies. That is why what we are seeing is a bit disturbing and destabilising development. Some of us are committed to a true leadership that will emerge from the Afenifere, that will look back and walk the path of the founding fathers such as the Awolowo, Ajasin, Adesanya and Adebanjo mould, especially the Adebanjo mould who followed through to the letter; progressivism. It saddens me greatly that Oba Olaitan, who presided over a meeting of the Afenifere at the country home of the leader, Pa Ayo Adebanjo, in which the whole body of the Afenifere faithful passed a vote of confidence on Pa Adebanjo’s leadership and promptly proclaimed Chief Ayo Adebanjo as the de facto leader and a press release to that effect signed by Oba Olaitan and the Secretary General was promptly issued, to now read from Oba Olaitan’s statement which totally removed the truest leader, Pa Ayo Adebanjo, from the list of his predecessors, simply smack of an act that could not be more ridiculous. Lastly, there is a huge fundamental gorge that exists between the Adebanjo group and the Fasoranti group. Let us not deceive ourselves that some people exploited Fasoranti at his most vulnerable period so well advanced in age, and these powerful people are with President Tinubu. How on earth would Oba Olaitan think that he would lead a united Afenifere? I think it would be a cheap trick to think that the Fasoranti group would gobble at it and simply fall over and allow Oba Olaitan to lead them. It is not going to happen. It is the Adebanjo faction of the Afenifere that is now aligned with the SDP. There is an arrangement that Afenifere will handle everything that has to do with the SDP in the South-West. A lot has happened in that regard. Who again will be thrown under the bus? Is it President Tinubu and his APC, or will it be Mr. Adewole Adebayo of the SDP that will be thrown under the bus? So, we are a long way from straight forward solution. I am just waiting for the time this whole exercise will begin to look ridiculous.” According to Adejumo, Adebanjo historically embodied the true, uncompromising ideals of the original Afenifere movement. He said: “Against this historical background, one can argue that, among those who claimed to represent the true ideals of Afenifere, Chief Ayo Adebanjo embodied those ideals particularly well. Chief Reuben Fasoranti himself reportedly captured this sentiment in his resignation letter, describing Adebanjo as the personification of Afenifere. When Fasoranti eventually left the scene, one could reasonably ask whether he had navigated the political situation successfully. After all, it was Adebanjo who had helped bring him into the leadership position in the first place.” Sharing a perspective of how Fasoranti emerged as Afenifere leader, Adejumo explained how Adebanjo declined to take the leadership position. He said: “This was not the first time Afenifere had faced the question of succession. When Chief Abraham Adesanya became seriously ill and suffered a stroke, he wanted to identify a successor. He called two senior Afenifere members, Olanihun Ajayi and Chief Ayo Adebanjo, and asked them to choose between themselves.” Ijebu mafia Adejumo explained further: “Adebanjo, however, declined to take the position. He explained that he and others from Ijebu had long been labelled the Ijebu mafia, a description he rejected. He worried that his emergence as leader might reinforce that perception and deepen divisions within the organisation. Instead, he proposed finding someone who was respected, approachable, and capable of bringing the different tendencies within Afenifere together without being immediately identified with a particular faction. When asked whom he had in mind, Adebanjo suggested Fasoranti. The suggestion initially surprised Adesanya, who did not immediately recall Fasoranti as a prominent member of the inner caucus. Adebanjo explained that Fasoranti had been involved with the organisation since 1953 and had served as Commissioner for Finance under Chief Michael Ajasin when Ajasin was governor of Ondo State. Fasoranti was not a member of the inner caucus, but that was precisely part of the attraction. He had not been at the forefront of the controversies surrounding the treasonable felony case, nor had he been among those most traumatised by the military repression associated with the Abacha era. At the time, he was a retired school principal, who was only managing his business. Adebanjo believed that someone with this background could provide the organisation with the kind of leadership capable of rallying together its different members. And so Fasoranti emerged as leader. Unfortunately, from around 2008, Afenifere entered a period of turbulence. The organisation struggled to maintain its momentum, while Fasoranti faced pressure from political forces that opposed his leadership. Those forces encouraged the emergence of competing figures, including Ayo Fasanmi, followed by Biyi Durojaiye and Chief Olusi, deepening the internal divisions. The situation troubled Fasoranti greatly. By 2015, he had reportedly had enough and was considering stepping aside. This was despite Afenifere’s significant contribution, alongside the Jonathan administration, to the 2014 National Conference. Once again, Adebanjo intervened and persuaded Fasoranti to continue. Meanwhile, Fasoranti was increasingly inclined to retire. Some members of his inner circle in Akure, Ondo State, were reportedly spreading claims that he was becoming senile, and there were concerns that some were positioning themselves to take control from him. Fasoranti therefore moved quickly and announced Adebanjo as acting leader. Many of us regarded this as one leader doing the right thing by another. Oba Olaitan was subsequently made deputy leader. Afenifere gained renewed visibility under Adebanjo. He became a prominent public voice, attracting new members and reviving the organization’s reputation as a principled political movement.” Support for Peter Obi in 2023 Adejumo noted: “As the 2023 presidential election approached, Adebanjo began consulting members about the organisation’s political position. The discussions had reportedly started as early as 2021 and continued over approximately two years. I was the Publicity Secretary at the time, and I participated alongside other members of the executive. Adebanjo’s argument was rooted in equity. He maintained that the Igbo had not yet had an opportunity to produce a Nigerian president, while the North and the Yoruba had each held the presidency for eight years. The South-South had also produced President Goodluck Jonathan, although his tenure was shorter than eight years. Adebanjo argued that Nigerians should consider giving the Igbo a chance. Equity, he believed, was an essential route to justice. His objective was a Nigeria in which no region felt permanently excluded from the nation’s highest office. That was how we rallied behind the presidential candidacy of Peter Obi. There is much more to say about that election, but one point deserves emphasis. Without Obi’s candidacy, President Bola Tinubu might not have become president. The votes Obi attracted in the seven states he won, together with the Federal Capital Territory, could otherwise have substantially strengthened Atiku Abubakar’s position against Tinubu. Given the historical voting patterns in the South-East, where the PDP had traditionally performed strongly, it is reasonable to argue that Obi’s emergence significantly altered the electoral contest. We must also acknowledge the longstanding tensions between the Yoruba and Igbo. I had previously tried to help bring the two groups closer together through Afenifere. That effort has not yet achieved all its objectives, but reconciliation remains a work in progress. In supporting Obi, Adebanjo was acting on his conviction that political equity could help strengthen national unity. Paradoxically, however, the votes Obi attracted may also have benefited President Tinubu by dividing the opposition vote. In that sense, one could argue that Adebanjo’s decision indirectly helped create the electoral conditions that enabled President Tinubu to win the presidency. Let us leave that debate for another occasion and turn to the present crisis. The post Fasoranti’s death: Rumbling in Yorubaland, a new Afenifere may emerge appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: US Court denies discovery request against Tinubu
items.description: By Johnbosco Agbakwuru ABUJA –The United States District Court for the District of Columbia has denied a motion by Aaron Greenspan seeking limited discovery from Nigerian President Bola Tinubu and DCI Group in ongoing litigation under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA). Special Adviser to the President on Information and Strategy, Bayo Onanuga, in a post on his X account stated that in its October 30 ruling, the Court determined that the proposed discovery concerning alleged cyberattacks on Greenspan’s website was not sufficiently relevant to the underlying FOIA dispute involving the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). “The Court’s decision makes clear that this Freedom of Information Act proceeding cannot be used to pursue discovery unrelated to the legal questions before it,” said attorney Christopher W. Carmichael. “By denying the request for discovery against President Tinubu and DCI Group, the Court reinforced the importance of keeping this litigation focused on the issues properly before it.” According to him, the Court also denied a separate motion by nonparty Karl Von Batten seeking permission to file an amicus curiae (friend-of-the-court) brief, as well as Greenspan’s related request for judicial notice. Additionally, the Court denied Greenspan’s motion for summary judgment. “The Court also denied the plaintiff’s motion for summary judgment and rejected a separate request to introduce an amicus brief,” said Attorney Oluwole Afolabi. “While the underlying FOIA issues remain before the Court, these rulings establish important procedural boundaries and clarify which matters are appropriate for consideration in this litigation.” The post US Court denies discovery request against Tinubu appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Gada launches Sokoto East Senate campaign, receives defectors
items.description: By Musa Ubandawaki, Sokoto SOKOTO — Former Senator Abubakar Umar Gada has declared the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) ready to reclaim political power in Sokoto State in 2027, following the defection of members of the All Progressives Congress (APC) and African Democratic Congress (ADC) to the party. Gada made the declaration on Saturday in Gwadabawa during the flag-off of his campaign for the Sokoto East Senatorial District seat, where he received the defectors and urged party supporters to mobilise ahead of the 2027 general elections. The former senator expressed confidence in the PDP’s prospects, describing Sokoto East as a traditional stronghold of the party despite its recent electoral setbacks. According to him, the PDP’s past electoral performance in the district provided a foundation for its anticipated comeback, adding that the party’s immediate task was to restore the confidence and determination of its supporters. “ SOKOTO East is traditionally a PDP zone. Past performance data and records have shown that. So, it is just to awaken them and bring back their self-consciousness, determination and readiness to take over,” Gada said. He maintained that his previous tenure in the Senate had equipped him with the experience and legislative accomplishments required to represent the district effectively. Gada said his record in the National Assembly distinguished him from other contenders seeking the seat. “I do not want to sound immodest, but I am always proud of my performance the last time I was in the Senate. People have recently made efforts, and I think they have done a lot, but compared to what we achieved at the time, it was absolutely incredible,” he said. Addressing the security and poverty challenges confronting communities in Sokoto East, Gada called for deliberate government intervention, strategic deployment of resources and increased federal attention to areas facing urgent developmental needs. He said the electorate deserved leadership capable of responding to insecurity, economic hardship and inadequate development, stressing that sustained government commitment was necessary to improve the living conditions of vulnerable communities. The PDP candidate also urged voters to defend their electoral rights and remain vigilant during the 2027 general elections, describing the ballot as a powerful instrument for determining their political future. “They are the power. Their votes are their guns and arsenals. Their voice is their weapon of battle. They should respect and understand that this is their God-given right,” he said. He warned that the consequences of electing unsuitable leaders could extend beyond the immediate electoral cycle, urging residents to make informed decisions based on their long-term interests and the future of their communities. Also speaking at the campaign flag-off, the PDP leader in Sokoto State and National Organising Secretary of the party, Umar Bature, described Gada as a credible candidate, citing his previous legislative tenure as evidence of his capacity to deliver on electoral promises. Bature expressed confidence in the party’s electoral prospects, declaring that the PDP was determined to reclaim the Sokoto State Government House and win the three senatorial districts in the 2027 elections. The campaign flag-off and reception of defectors from the APC and ADC come as political parties begin preparations for the 2027 general elections in Sokoto State. The post Gada launches Sokoto East Senate campaign, receives defectors appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: SMOKERS’ CORNER: THE MYTH OF PTI’S POPULARITY
items.description: For years, political analysts across the board, from pro-Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) commentators to supposedly neutral and anti-PTI observers, insisted that PTI was the most popular political party in the country. This narrative was even widely echoed by Western media outlets. Lately, however, that conviction has eroded. Commentators first began backtracking by limiting their claims about PTI’s dominance to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP), but even that has started to falter. What many mistook for widespread support may simply have been what political scientists refer to as “manufactured popularity.” Manufactured popularity is not a reflection of unmediated public sentiment. Instead, it is a carefully crafted construct accumulated through symbolic engineering, media management, state or institutional sponsorship, and the strategic exploitation of public disillusionment. At its core, manufactured popularity depends on presenting a leader as a spotless saviour, who is capable of dismantling a ‘corrupt’ old order. This form of popularity is built on exaggerated promises and carefully curated media narratives. But the moment an engineered project makes the transition from opposition to executive power, tensions between rhetoric and governance begin to dissolve the illusion. Throughout history, political regimes and movements have demonstrated how manufactured popularity can decay when confronted with cold realities. In the 1950s, former president Juan Perón’s initial popularity in Argentina was sustained by heavy state subsidies and nationalistic appeals. Yet, as economic historian Carlos Díaz-Alejandro documented in his analyses of Argentine economic history, the regime’s inability to sustain fiscal extravagance amidst soaring inflation and foreign exchange depletion eventually caused Perón’s populist economic model to unravel, hastening widespread unrest and military intervention. While PTI’s online dominance is often taken as proof of overwhelming public support, digital visibility, electoral success and the ability to mobilise people on the streets are three very different measures of political strength In post-communist Eastern Europe, the rise and fall of political movements that relied on media-driven anti-corruption narratives, such as Simeon Saxe-Coburg-Gotha’s movement in Bulgaria during the early 2000s, illustrate that popularity constructed primarily on outsider status and high moral claims quickly evaporates when administrative ineptitude and economic compromises take hold in daily governance. PTI, formed by Imran Khan in 1996, is an intriguing example. It remained a minor player on the margins of Pakistani politics till its transformation into a dominant force in 2011. The transformation was not merely an ‘awakening’ but also a carefully constructed political phenomenon. PTI’s popularity was methodically cultivated, mainly by the military establishment. Indeed, the party effectively mobilised a real sense of grievance among urban middle-class voters who were exhausted by the perceived ‘corruption’ of traditional parties such as the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP). But this was amplified by institutional engineering through a hybrid scheme. According to the Pakistani political scholar Muhammad Waseem, in this scheme, intelligence agencies steered the media narrative, weakened political opponents, and directed influential political “electables” towards PTI. Illustration by Abro The architecture of PTI’s popularity was heavily built on a modern communication strategy. According to the media researcher Ifrah Nadeem, PTI pioneered the use of “computational propaganda.” It unleashed tightly targeted social media campaigns, and emotional messaging. By leveraging digital spaces, the party bypassed mainstream journalistic scrutiny, portraying Khan as an incorruptible reformer who alone could usher in a ‘Naya [New] Pakistan.’ According to economists such as Atif Mian and academic assessments by the International Crisis Group, governing a state such as Pakistan that is under severe balance-of-payments distress required unpopular policy adjustments. But this contradicted PTI’s idealised campaign claims. So, when Khan was placed in power in 2018, the election of an ‘honest leader’ was framed by the party as a good enough condition for economic revival and institutional purification. But Khan blundered his way across almost all vital areas of governance. This resulted in the gradual pullback of the military establishment’s patronage of his regime. Therefore, the manufactured framework sustaining the government collapsed, culminating in Khan’s removal via a constitutional vote of no-confidence in 2022. The erosion of manufactured popularity reveals a recurring dynamic in politics. According to the American political scientist Samuel P. Huntington, while media manipulation, emotional appeals and institutional patronage can create an impression of overwhelming public approval, they cannot transform into tangible administrative competence and economic stability. While failing leaders who were elevated through manufactured popularity often switch to narratives of victimisation or conspiracy to retain a dedicated core, the initial perception of popularity begins to alter when tested by on-ground political realities. But here’s the interesting bit: even after Khan’s fall, the narrative of his ‘popularity’ did not recede as such. At least not in the media. Political commentators and international monitoring groups viewed the support for PTI-backed candidates in the 2024 general elections as proof of this. However, one can posit that this was largely achieved through PTI’s formal and informal social media apparatus transitioning the party’s narrative from that of producing an incorruptible saviour to one of moral victimisation. In the aftermath of Khan’s arrest in 2023, PTI’s media apparatus cleverly converted the general public anger over rising inflation and political instability (which Khan’s regime left behind), into an unquestioning loyalty to the imprisoned Khan. This was further reinforced by digital algorithms that amplified symbolic/performative acts of resistance, creating an impression of impressive public mobilisation. However, the eventual reality check occurred when the limits of this online and sentiment-based popularity were tested on the ground. The definitive moment arrived when the current coalition government-imposed emergency measures and governor’s rule in KP recently, sidelining PTI’s provincial government there. Contrary to expectations of an uprising, the public response was muted. The failure of the party to mobilise street demonstrations underscored a disconnect between online sentiment and real-life capacity. This led political analysts to re-evaluate the nature of the party’s popular base. They began recognising that much of what had been interpreted as deep political commitment was, in fact, passive sympathy, digital noise, and an anti-establishment protest vote rather than an organised, resilient political movement. The illusion of overwhelming popularity unravels when passive sympathisers who express support on social media or through voting, decline to transform into active political actors on the streets. They are in the majority, and many are even stationed abroad. The loss of PTI’s last institutional foothold in KP demonstrates that, while manufactured popularity and grievance-based narratives can maintain an electoral pull, they remain inherently fragile when confronted with state power, and the reality of growing public apathy. The electoral pull too is now likely to recede, especially with the likelihood of Khan remaining behind bars in the foreseeable future. Published in Dawn, EOS, November 1st, 2026

items.title: ‘Medicine pricing needs serious attention’
items.description: KARACHI: More than 86,000 medicines produced by pharmaceutical companies have been registered under the Track and Trace System, allowing consumers to scan products by mobile phone to check their authenticity and find out their prices, Federal Health Minister Mustafa Kamal said. He said that pharmaceutical companies could also register their medicines and products online. A process that previously took years is now being completed within just 21 days. Addressing the members of the Korangi Association of Trade and Industry (KATI) on Saturday, he said the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (DRAP) has been made fully transparent and digitalised. Eight months had passed since DRAP’s certification procedures were shifted to a digital system, during which more than 5,000 cases had been processed, he said. Mustafa Kamal said the issue of medicine pricing requires serious attention. The pharmaceutical industries seek an increase in medicine prices, but the matter is under consideration by the federal cabinet. The issue has two dimensions as an increase in medicine prices will create additional financial difficulties for ordinary citizens, while keeping prices unchanged could lead to shortages of medicines for serious illnesses. Consequently, patients were sometimes forced to purchase the same medicines from the black market at three times their actual price. Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

items.title: Nuclear science boosts Pakistan’s ability to track groundwater
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Pakistan has strengthened its ability to track groundwater resources using nuclear science, enabling scientists to identify recharge sources, determine groundwater age and trace contamination pathways, according to an International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) report released on Saturday. The Regional Cooperative Agree­ment (RCA) for Research, Deve­lopment and Training Related to Nuclear Science and Technology for Asia and the Pacific, Hydrology and Groundwater programme has significantly enhanced Pakistan’s capacity for continuous groundwater monitoring through the application of isotope-based techniques. This advancement has considerably strengthened the connection between scientific research and water governance, allowing for more precise and systematic observation of groundwater dynamics across diverse hydrogeological settings, the IAEA report said. Studies undertaken through RCA-supported projects have generated reliable estimates of groundwater recharge rates, aquifer interconnections and pollution pathways in key regions such as the Indus Plain, the Quetta Valley and the Cholistan Desert. IAEA report says RCA-backed isotope techniques help country trace water sources, age, pollution pathways These findings have deepened the scientific understanding of Pakistan’s groundwater systems while providing essential inputs for developing long-term strategies for water reso­urce management, the agency noted. Prior to joining the programme, groundwater monitoring was not a primary focus of national hydrological investigations. Several studies were conducted using conventional methods, such as hydro-chemical analyses and physical measurements, but these approaches provided only basic information on water table depth, water quality and aquifer dynamics. Through its participation in the programme, Pakistan has significantly strengthened its laboratory capacity for isotope hydrology. The Pakistan Institute of Nuclear Science and Technology (Pinstech) now hosts one of the region’s most advanced isotope analysis facilities, complemented by 12 laboratories nationwide. Currently, Pinstech and the Pakistan Council of Research in Water Resources work in close collaboration to incorporate isotopic data into national groundwater management models. “This integration supports the early detection of over-extraction, salinity intrusion and other forms of aquifer stress, thereby contributing to more sustainable groundwater utilisation,” the report said. The focus on data-driven management has fostered a stronger culture of evidence-based decision-making within national and provincial water institutions. Policymakers are increasingly rel­ying on isotope hydrology data to inf­orm regulatory frameworks, resource allocation and long-term planning, reflecting a significant shift from reactive to preventive and science-informed groundwater management. Pakistan’s participation has delivered substantial economic, social and environmental benefits. Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026
