items.title: The Rise of the Tallboy Is a Sign of the Times
items.description: Say you’re at a football game (fun!), in large part for the food (correct!). You have spent your time at the stadium successfully curating an alfresco fine-dining experience: the pregame amuse-bouche (popcorn, maybe, with a swirl of let’s-agree-to-call-it-butter), the first-quarter aperitif (a frosty can of beer), the second-quarter appetizer (a plate of fries, doused with ketchup), the third-quarter entrée (nachos, obviously, washed down with a second beer). It’s now the fourth quarter, and although the game has gone as planned (probably? you haven’t been paying tons of attention), your dessert course has not. The menu options before you—churro, cotton candy—are leaving you stymied. That is possibly because, you come to realize, you are unexpectedly drunk. It might have been the beer. But it also might have been the beer’s packaging: the vessel sometimes called a pint can and sometimes called a pounder but typically known as a tallboy. Tallboys resemble everyday cans—they definitely are everyday cans—but they are also sneaky in their canniness. Instead of the standard can’s 12 ounces of liquid, they hold 16. And in sports stadiums around the country, they are becoming ever more common. The beer, like so much else, is getting bigger. One result: Even if you’re having just two cans of the stuff, you could be getting much more booze than you bargained for. Tallboys have their reasons. At sporting events in particular, larger servings—of drinks, of food, of whatever—tend to mean fewer trips to the concession stand, a convenient thing if you happen to be attending the game to watch the action on the field. And tallboys give distributors, be they brewers or store owners or stadium operators, a similar bang for their buck. Though the larger cans cost only marginally more to produce than the typical 12-ouncers, their added capacity means that sellers can offer them at a much higher price. And because tallboys were for a long time associated primarily with microbrews, they retain some of the latent cachet of craft beer, whether the beverage inside is a malty masterpiece or (and I say this with love) 16 ounces of musty hop water. [ Read: The bad beer that’s an incredible beverage ] The cans themselves are going macro: “Hundreds of thousands of tallboys will be brought to the stadium each week,” Nebraska Public Media reported last year, as the University of Nebraska Cornhuskers—and their fans—prepared for the coming season. The shipments included both local craft beers and decidedly less local domestic ones; Molson Coors and Anheuser-Busch, the respective makers of Coors and Budweiser, offer their own brews in 16-ounce formats. The triumph of the tallboy is in one way unsurprising. (If you’re an American marketer, you’ll rarely go wrong assuming that bigger products are better products.) But the cans’ ubiquity has also exposed the many flaws in what you might call the tallboy user experience. Some are blandly logistical. At the stadium, the same thing that might help minimize lines at the concession stand (more liquid per can) can also lead to, uh, longer lines at the restroom. And the larger cans, unless you resort to guzzling, nearly guarantee that the ice-cold beer you’ve bought at a stadium-friendly premium—your amber waves of grain, your American dream in a pop-top can—will end in a tepid nightmare. These may be divisive times, but one of the few things Americans can still agree on is that we deserve better than warm beer. Those design flaws pale in comparison, however, to a bigger one: Tallboys are containers for alcohol that offer one-and-a-third times the alcohol most consumers are used to. If you’re aiming for inebriation, their size—their undeniable efficiency as booze-delivery vehicles—works in your favor. (It works especially well when the tallboys are vessels for craft beers, which typically feature a higher alcohol content than Bud and Coors.) If you’re not looking for drunkenness, though, the tallboy could lead you there anyway, and quite unexpectedly. It could create a situation in which, say, the ballpark banquet you’ve been enjoying ends not with a Cracker Jack bang but a slightly slurred whimper. Beer connoisseurs may pay attention to the alcohol content listed on cans; for everyone else, though, a can tends to imply a single serving, whatever the numbers say. No wonder tallboys are becoming, as one blog put it , “infamous.” With booze as with so much else, even small changes in packaging and design can have cascading impacts on consumers. The 12-ounce can was never the only option, beer vessel–wise (see: the pixie-size, 8-ounce can known as the “stubbie”; the 19.2-ounce “stovepipe”; the 24-ounce “silo,” also known as—yep—the “tallerboy”). Still, for decades, it has been the default. The earliest beer cans, created in the 1930s and made of coated steel, were 12-ouncers. Their design evolved over the decades (the shift to aluminum, the advent of ring-pull openers), but their size, for the most part, did not. And their size— no can is an island , John Donne might have said—shaped everything else, including national supply chains (shipping pallets, calibrated to move cans roughly 4.8 inches tall) and Etsy-fied cottage industries (beer koozies, made to wrap snugly around cans 2.6 inches wide). Along the way, the cans’ size has also affected Americans’ expectations of what a single serving of beer entails. Since the 1980s, the U.S. government’s dietary guidelines have defined a “standard-size drink” as 5 ounces of wine, 1.5 ounces of distilled spirits, or 12 ounces of beer. [ Read: Canned cocktails will smash you to the ground ] Tallboys bring chaos to the whole system. They take that basic premise, a can of beer , and make it a little less straightforward.They’re similar, in that way, to other containers—a tub of Ben & Jerry’s, for example, whose literal pint size tends to belie the multiple servings contained therein. The main difference, of course, is the alcohol. And that’s another reason tallboys are becoming a bit infamous. They assume that people want a little more when many, in this age of rising sobriety and GLP-1s , want a little less. They’re repackaging alcohol when drinking, for a wide share of consumers, is losing its appeal . But they are also signs of the times. Tallboys may be gaining traction, in part, because they lend themselves so nicely to sales beyond the stadium. Even as overall alcohol consumption declines, the venues selling alcohol are expanding. Recent years have seen a growing number of grocery, convenience, and big-box stores adding alcohol to their offerings. The extended marketplace has turned beer cans, even more than before, into branding opportunities. Whatever the brew inside might have to offer, the beer’s packaging (neon coloring! punny names!) is a big element of the pitch. Because of that, for the people who sell them, tallboys are bigger cans that may really amount to better ones: larger canvases that are more likely than their smaller cousins to catch consumers’ eyes. The bigger cans also bring a certain literalism to the idea of the single-serving beer. Tallboys mimic the pint glass—the 16-ounce serving you’d typically get at a bar. And though they are sometimes sold in packs (four cans, typically, as opposed to the traditional six), many stores offer them for individual sale: convenient grab-and-go options meant to be bought, and consumed, one by one. Six-packs? Cases? Those are packaging options meant for parties. The solo tallboy assumes that you’ll be getting your buzz on alone, something that more Americans—among those who still drink— are doing . Maybe that’s another reason for tallboys’ encroaching infamy. These tall cans are tidy metaphors: for little changes that become big ones, for casual maximalism, for a culture contending with rampant isolation. They are, in other words, single-serving containers that capture something about the way we live now—even if they contain a product that tastes better in company.

items.title: Capt Safdar's remarks about women suffering from illness draw criticism, including from CM Maryam
items.description: LAHORE: Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz’s spouse, retired Capt Muhammad Safdar, has come under fire for disparaging remarks about women advocating for bodily autonomy. Speaking at a Khatm-i-Nabuwwat rally in Chiniot earlier this week, Safdar took aim at the slogan “ mera jism, meri marzi ” (my body, my choice). He questioned why women who assert control over their bodies turn to religious scholars for prayers when diagnosed with serious illnesses such as cancer. “They say, ‘My body, my choice.’ But when they fall ill or develop cancer, they turn to religious scholars, seeking prayers and blessed water for a cure. They should understand that if they claim ownership over their bodies, they should also be able to cure them. In reality, the human body is under God’s control,” he said. On Friday, Maryam responded to a post on X regarding the speech, which stated: “Maryam Nawaz’s husband, Captain Safdar, also lost his mother-in-law to cancer, yet here he is mocking women who are battling cancer.” The chief minister’s mother, Kulsoom Nawaz, passed away in 2018 after a months-long battle with cancer. “Heartbreaking,” the chief minister said, posting an emoji of a broken heart. “The silent battles a woman, a wife, fights behind closed doors … The strength she must find even when she feels like breaking. Some battles are fought in silence and some wounds are invisible,” she said. Apart from CM Maryam, users on social media also took issue with Safdar’s remarks. “My [mother] has been a cancer patient, and God knows how we managed to get through those difficult times. Her survival was nothing short of a miracle. Listening to Capt Safdar’s remarks on this matter is utterly shameful and disgraceful!” said TV anchor Ajmal Jami on X. He also thanked CM Maryam for her “thoughtful and compassionate words for all those brave women”. Another user, Maheen Ghani, said: “So a woman who says ‘ mera jism, meri marzi ’, which is essentially about autonomy and consent, loses the right to ask for prayers when she gets cancer? Is that seriously the argument? “To take a woman’s illness, her fear and her faith and turn them into an opportunity to humiliate her. What an ugly, twisted understanding of both women’s rights and religion.” On the other hand, some, like journalist Benazir Shah, lauded CM Maryam for speaking out. “It takes real courage to take a public stand like this. More power to you, Maryam Nawaz Sharif,” she said. Lawyers’ bodies condemn remarks about Asma Jahangir Meanwhile, two premier lawyers’ bodies on Saturday strongly condemned Safdar for his remarks about Asma Jahangir – a renowned senior lawyer and human rights activist who passed away in 2018. During the rally, Safdar had called the late lawyer “cursed”. Pakistan Bar Council (PBC) Vice Chairman Pir Muhammad Masood Chishti, as well as the 28th executive committee of the outgoing Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA), regretted the remarks and urged public representatives to exercise restraint and uphold dignity in their statements. Chishti called upon the relevant authorities to take immediate notice and initiate appropriate legal action. “The use of disparaging language and references to her religious identity to malign her is highly regrettable and deserves strong condemnation,” the PBC vice chairman regretted, adding that making such remarks against a deceased woman, who was no longer alive to defend herself or respond, was particularly “deplorable and reflects a lack of decency and respect”. The PBC vice chairman observed that differences of opinion must never become a pretext for personal attacks, hate speech, character assassination or religious intolerance. “The invaluable services and contributions of the late Asma Jahangir to the legal fraternity, human rights and the rule of law deserve respect and recognition,” he emphasised. Likewise, the 28th executive committee of the SCBA strongly and unanimously took exception to the recent remarks by Safdar. “These remarks are highly condemnable and have deeply wounded the sentiments of the entire legal community,” the SCBA said, adding that Jahangir was a devout Muslim who dedicated her life to justice, humanity, and the rights of all people, without discrimination. “Her services to humanity and human rights transcended religious boundaries and to make such hateful remarks about her was not only deeply disrespectful but also an insult to all those who continue to honour her legacy. She stood for the rights of every individual without discrimination.” The SCBA also strongly condemned derogatory remarks by Safdar against women and an illness that was “being valiantly fought back by hundreds of thousands of women across the world”. “At a time when women are breaking barriers, such remarks are disgraceful and entirely unacceptable,” the SCBA said. “What makes this conduct even more shameful is that his own spouse holds the highest office of Punjab chief minister, and he himself is the father of a daughter; he should have been ashamed of making such insensitive and degrading remarks directed against the women,” it said. These statements may also attract penal consequences, the SCBA reminded and called upon the concerned authorities to take immediate and strict notice and proceed in accordance with the law. “Such divisive, offensive, and intolerant attitudes must be firmly challenged and nipped in the bud. “Let it be clear to all and sundry, we will not remain silent when the dignity of our legal fraternity, the legacy of a human rights champion, and the respect owed to women are attacked,” the SCBA statement said. Nasir Iqbal from Islamabad also contributed to this report.

items.title: Crypto exchanges call for quick moves to bolster defences after Binance heist
items.description: Crypto exchanges are taking quick action to bolster their defences and urging greater industry-wide information-sharing after a record $6.3 billion hack of Binance exposed their vulnerability just as they become more embedded in mainstream finance. Coinbase said it made adjustments to its systems that store cryptocurrency keys offline “solely out of an abundance of caution”, while Kraken said it was monitoring industry incidents for lessons it could apply to its defences. But the industry will need to move urgently, analysts and industry executives said, as United States President Donald Trump’s regulators promote deeper integration of digital assets into the financial system, raising the stakes for an industry with a history of big hacks. “For crypto to reach its full potential, the security situation must be addressed immediately,” said Chris Perkins, Franklin Templeton’s head of crypto. Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, halted withdrawals after Thursday’s attack , which analysts blamed on North Korea and said it would use company funds to cover the losses. Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said on X that the complex attack may have begun with a compromised software engineer’s laptop, giving hackers access to systems used to process withdrawals. The company later found additional breaches, while software designed to erase traces of the attack hampered the investigation. Rival crypto exchanges moved quickly on Friday to shore up their own systems and to reassure customers that their tokens were safe. Full-time teams at Kraken look for potential vulnerabilities every day, a Kraken spokesperson said. Still, even as the industry reeled from the biggest cryptocurrency heist of all time, executives expressed confidence that Binance had sufficient resources to cover the losses and that the hack would not have broader financial repercussions. Bitcoin fell more than 4 per cent on Thursday while ether, the second-largest cryptocurrency, fell more than 5pc, although both tokens recovered some of that ground on Friday. “Our expectation is the industry writ large will actually not suffer material losses, even though Binance is obviously going to have to deal with the exploit directly,” said Josh Riezman, chief legal and strategy officer at crypto firm GSR. The bulk of the heist unfolded in around 20 minutes late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis. North Korea routinely denies involvement in cryptocurrency thefts, and its mission in Geneva did not respond to requests for comment. Hack involves social engineering, money laundering While much remains unclear, social engineering, a common tactic in which hackers trick victims into revealing sensitive information or granting access to systems, may have been involved in compromising the laptop, security experts said. Harry Donnelly, CEO of Circuit, a crypto risk infrastructure company, said companies are planning more employee training to guard against social engineering attacks. In such attacks, hackers race to launder the funds before the exchange detects the breach and token issuers freeze assets. Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57bn linked to Binance, while Circle said it froze $800 million. Bitcoin and ether cannot be frozen because no single entity controls the coins. Chainalysis said the hackers appeared to be using sophisticated laundering patterns it had not seen before. On Friday, some crypto exchange executives called for the industry to develop a coordinated hack detection system. “We need a real-time alert system that allows participants to share information immediately when a hack occurs, coordinate a rapid response, and temporarily freeze suspected stolen funds,” said Star Xu, CEO of crypto exchange OKX, in a post on X. GSR’s Riezman added that the Binance hack could spur the industry to act: “As we’re at this kind of confluence moment for traditional finance and digital assets, I think it’s obviously important that we continue to improve, and I think this, if anything, will be a catalyst for that.”

L’annonce a été faite samedi par la gendarmerie. Cette intervention fait suite à un signalement faisant état de la présence de colis suspects sur ladite plage. items.title: Dori : Un homme condamné à la prison à perpétuité pour avoir défiguré sa compagne enceinte
items.description: Un homme a été condamné à la réclusion criminelle à perpétuité, le vendredi 30 octobre 2026, par la chambre criminelle du Tribunal de grande instance (TGI) de Dori, pour des faits de coups et blessures volontaires criminels sur sa compagne enceinte. Selon un communiqué du procureur du Faso près le TGI de Dori, la victime avait été grièvement blessée à l’arme blanche et défigurée à l’acide, dans la nuit du 31 août 2026. Les faits remontent au 1er septembre 2026, lorsque le Commissariat central de police de Dori a signalé la découverte d’une jeune femme grièvement blessée et inconsciente à Torodi, un village situé à une dizaine de kilomètres de la ville. Secourue puis évacuée au Centre hospitalier régional (CHR) de Dori, elle présentait de graves brûlures au visage, à la poitrine et aux mains, ainsi que des blessures sur plusieurs parties du corps. D’après les premiers éléments de l’enquête, les sévices auraient été infligés dans la nuit du 31 août 2026 à l’aide d’un produit acide et d’un objet contondant, notamment un couteau. Un communiqué administratif a permis de retrouver la famille de la victime trois jours après les faits. Après avoir repris connaissance, la jeune femme a désigné son compagnon comme étant l’auteur présumé de l’agression. Elle a expliqué aux enquêteurs qu’étant tombée enceinte de lui, ce dernier lui aurait demandé d’interrompre volontairement la grossesse. Face à son refus, il l’aurait attirée, par des stratagèmes, dans un endroit isolé, où il l’aurait rouée de coups, blessée au dos avec un couteau et aspergée d’acide au visage, la défigurant. Il l’aurait ensuite abandonnée sur place après qu’elle eut perdu connaissance. Elle n’a été secourue que le lendemain matin, de justesse. Grâce à la collaboration des populations, le mis en cause a été interpellé le 15 octobre 2026. Présenté au parquet le 20 octobre, il a été placé sous mandat de dépôt le même jour, dans l’attente de son jugement. Traduit devant la chambre criminelle du TGI de Dori le 30 octobre 2026, l’accusé a été reconnu coupable des faits qui lui étaient reprochés et condamné à la réclusion criminelle à perpétuité, sur le fondement de l’article 512-22 du Code pénal, selon le procureur du Faso, Sibiri Soumaïla Sanou. Dans son communiqué, le procureur a salué le professionnalisme et l’engagement du personnel soignant du CHR de Dori, auquel il attribue le sauvetage de la victime. Il a également félicité les acteurs de la chaîne pénale, en particulier l’unité de police judiciaire, ainsi que les populations pour leur contribution à l’interpellation du condamné. Minute.bf

items.title: La Tunisie va-t-elle enfin reconnaître la marocanité du Sahara occidental ?
items.description: Le Conseil de sécurité des Nations Unies n’a pas, lors de sa réunion tenue le vendredi 30 octobre 2026, procédé à la prorogation du mandat de la Mission des Nations unies pour l’organisation d’un référendum au Sahara occidental (Minurso). «Il s’agit là d’une évolution importante et d’une étape hautement significative vers la clôture définitive du dossier du Sahara marocain au sein des instances des Nations Unies», a souligné un communiqué du Cabinet Royal à Rabat. Nonobstant le veto opposé par la Russie au texte onusien, soutenu par onze membres du Conseil. Le Pakistan, la Chine et la Somalie s'étant, eux, abstenus. «Cette évolution marquante (…) consacre une rupture dans la gestion de ce dossier, marquant le passage d’une simple logique de gestion à une approche fondée sur une transformation profonde des paramètres» , ajoute le communiqué royal . Pour le Maroc, la non-reconduction de la mission de la Minurso signifie clairement que la présence de cette mission dans le sud du royaume – notamment à travers ses effectifs, ses véhicules, ses équipements et ses symboles — «devra prendre fin dans les jours à venir.» «C’est une page de 35 ans qui est désormais tournée. Cette mission, héritée d’un contexte révolu, a longtemps servi d’instrument pour internationaliser le différend régional relatif au recouvrement légitime, par le Royaume du Maroc, de ses provinces sahariennes» , souligne Rabat. Par ailleurs, la non-reconduction de la mission de la Minurso «devrait mettre un terme à la saisine du Conseil de sécurité sur ce dossier et entraîner le retrait de cette question de son ordre du jour. Dès lors, il ne subsistera plus aucune justification pour la tenue des réunions périodiques du Conseil consacrées au Sahara occidental, ni pour les rapports y afférents du Secrétaire général des Nations Unies, ni pour les exposés de son Envoyé personnel» , souligne Rabat. «Ainsi prend fin le processus politique onusien, qui a été malheureusement marqué par les manœuvres dilatoires des autres parties, leur insistance à créer une impasse et leur volonté de pérenniser le statu quo. Des démarches analogues seront, par ailleurs, entreprises très prochainement au sein d’autres instances des Nations Unies» , lit-on encore dans le même communiqué. Rabat exprime ainsi sa satisfaction face à cette évolution, tout en se disant «fermement attaché au cessez-le-feu, dans le respect absolu de son intégrité territoriale, de sa sécurité nationale et de la quiétude de ses citoyens.» Et en espérantque la dynamique internationale ainsi impulsée se poursuivra aux niveaux bilatéral et régional. «Cette dynamique a, en effet, permis de mobiliser un soutien important ; plus des deux tiers des États membres de l’Organisation des Nations Unies — parmi lesquels figurent des membres permanents du Conseil de sécurité et des puissances internationales influentes — soutiennent clairement l’initiative d’autonomie, dans le cadre de la souveraineté marocaine, en tant que seul cadre pour la résolution de ce différend régional» , souligne le communiqué royal marocain. Il reste à se demander si la Tunisie va prendre note de cette évolution et réviser sa position relative à la question du Sahara Occidental, ou continuer à affirmer ne pas prendre parti entre les différentes thèses en présence (souveraineté marocaine contre autodétermination du Front Polisario soutenue par l’Algérie). Rappelons qu’en août 2022, la visite du chef du Front Polisario, Brahim Ghali, invité par le président Kaïs Saïed à l’occasion du sommet de la Ticad 8 à Tunis, a provoqué une grave crise diplomatique avec le Maroc, qui a immédiatement rappelé son ambassadeur, suivi par le rappel du représentant tunisien par Tunis. Bien que la Tunisie ait réaffirmé sa neutralité, ce geste a été perçu par Rabat comme un alignement diplomatique en faveur de l’Algérie (qui soutient le Front Polisario), laissant les relations politiques entre Tunis et Rabat dans un état de gel prolongé. La Tunisie va-t-elle prendre acte des derniers développements en faveur de l a «Marocanité du Sahara» , reconnue par la plupart de ses partenaires, notamment occidentaux, et à leur tête les Etats-Unis et la France, pour tenter de rétablir les relations d’amitié et de fraternité qui la lie historiquement au Maroc, ou va-t-elle continuer à jouer la carte d’une soi-disant neutralité qui n’est clairement plus d’actualité ? Attendons voir… I. B. L’article La Tunisie va-t-elle enfin reconnaître la marocanité du Sahara occidental ? est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: AI-based attendance system leads to dismissal of 72 doctors in Balochistan
items.description: QUETTA: The Balochistan Health Department on Saturday dismissed 72 doctors from government service for prolonged absence from duty. The doctors were dismissed under an artificial intelligence (AI)-based attendance system introduced by the provincial government to ensure that medical staff reported for duty regularly. According to an official notification issued by the Balochistan health secretary, the action was taken under Section 4(B)(viii) of the Balochistan Employees’ Efficiency and Disciplinary Act (BEEDA), 2011. The notification said the medical officers (BPS-17) and senior medical officers (BPS-18) had been dismissed from service with immediate effect on account of their unauthorised absence from government duty. The dismissal orders were issued with immediate effect, according to the notification. The total number of employees dismissed from the Health Department has now reached 200. Health Department officials said Rs410 million had so far been deducted from employees’ salaries over absenteeism. The notification added that notices had been issued to 11,000 employees, seeking explanations for violations of attendance and disciplinary rules. “Departmental action is under way against another 800 employees,” it said. In a statement, Balochistan Health Minister Bakht Muhammad Kakar said the doctors had repeatedly been issued notices directing them to report for duty, but they had failed to respond. Their continued absence from duty and failure to respond to repeated notices had compelled the government to take action, he added. “We have zero tolerance for absenteeism and negligence among medical staff and doctors in the performance of their official duties,” Kakar said, adding that the Health Department was making efforts to provide people with the best possible healthcare facilities at their doorsteps. He said reforms were under way to improve the performance of the provincial Health Department on the instructions of Chief Minister Mir Sarfraz Bugti. He added that staff attendance at government hospitals and health centres was being monitored through an AI-based attendance system.

items.title: Fact Check: Colombia gym video falsely linked to earthquake in Xizang
items.description: A video showing people fleeing a shaking building was falsely shared on social media as footage of the magnitude-7.0 earthquake that struck southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region in October. Fact Hunter traced the clip to a gym in Pereira, Colombia, filmed in August, nearly two months before the earthquake even happened. While the misleading posts only racked up around 81,000 views, the tactic of repackaging old footage as breaking news is a growing concern. Claim On October 23, X user @tparon posted a video showing a building shaking as people evacuated down a staircase. The post claimed it was the first video to emerge from China following the earthquake in Xizang, falsely stating it captured the moment the disaster struck. However, an examination of the video's publication history, location details and the buildings visible in the footage found that it had no connection to the earthquake in China. Fact Check 1. The video was published before the Xizang earthquake The footage appeared on the Instagram account of Meta Gym, a fitness center in Colombia, as early as August 12, 2026, during a period of seismic activity in the country. The gym's post identified the location as its Parque Industrial branch. The original video runs about 71 seconds, more than twice the length of the 34-second version later circulated on X. Related footage also appeared on YouTube and Facebook that same day, providing further evidence that the clip predated the October earthquake. 2. The gym's sign matches a location in Colombia Visual details provide another clue to its origin. The building's facade displays a distinctive sign featuring the word "meta" in white, a yellow letter "B" and the word "GYM" on the right. The logo matches that of Meta Gym, a fitness center in Colombia. The gym's August Instagram post showed the same damaged premises. Its official Facebook account also listed the address of its Parque Industrial branch, consistent with the location identified in the Instagram post. A search for Meta Gym in Pereira on Google Maps led to the corresponding building in Google Street View. Its location near Parque Industrial matched the gym's listed address. Further comparisons showed that the gym's sign, the building's exterior colors and a light-colored multi-storey building to its right were all consistent with images captured by Google Street View in 2024. 3. Daylight conditions contradict the claimed timing The lighting in the footage also contradicts the claim that it showed the moment the Xizang earthquake struck. According to monitoring data from the Xizang Earthquake Agency, the magnitude-7.0 earthquake occurred at 10:33 p.m. Beijing time on October 22. The video, by contrast, clearly shows daylight conditions. Footage of the earthquake published by Euronews on October 23 showed nighttime conditions when the tremor occurred. 4. How the misleading video spread The footage circulated in two main waves: first on August 12 and again on October 23. After its initial publication by Meta Gym, the video resurfaced on X following the earthquake in Xizang. Accounts including @tparon and @RoyaNewsEnglish shared English-language posts linking it to the disaster, while @LaHoraMX and @larepublica_co circulated Spanish-language versions. The misleading footage also appeared in Japanese- and Hindi-language posts, as well as on TikTok and Instagram. Spanish outlet Libertad Digital embedded the original misleading X post in its earthquake report, which brought the footage to a wider audience. Fact Hunter found that X user @chematierra has since deleted the misleading video and issued a correction. However, several other accounts left their posts linking the footage to the earthquake in Xizang online. 5. Account analysis The account that initially drew attention to the footage on October 23, @tparon, had approximately 15,500 followers on X. Its profile describes its focus as breaking news, natural disasters, police scanner activity, flights, open-source intelligence and conflicts. It regularly shares updates about events around the world. Background A magnitude-7.0 earthquake struck Baqen County in Nagqu City, Xizang Autonomous Region, at 10:33 p.m. on October 22, at a depth of 10 kilometers. The earthquake killed 16 people and injured 76, according to local government. Verdict: out of context The video is unrelated to the October 2026 Xizang earthquake. It had been publicly available since at least August 12 and showed an evacuation at Meta Gym's Parque Industrial branch in Pereira, Colombia. The gym's branding, building and surrounding environment matched the location identified through its social media accounts and Google Street View. The daylight conditions captured in the footage also contradict the nighttime timing of the earthquake in China. Conclusion This case illustrates how old footage can be repackaged as breaking news during a major disaster and spread across platforms and languages. When encountering videos claiming to show the scene of a recent disaster, viewers should check when the footage first appeared, compare identifiable landmarks and verify the location against reliable sources, rather than relying solely on captions or the images themselves.

items.title: Top scientists debate AI at World Laureates Forum
items.description: Top-tier scientists and trailblazers gathered in Shanghai on Saturday for the 2026 World Laureates Forum – a chance to pick each other's brains on future semiconductors, biomedicine, aerospace information, AI, future energy and quantum science. The eminent crowd includes 32 recipients of international honors like the Nobel Prize, Turing Award, Wolf Prize and Fields Medal, alongside 23 members of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Chinese Academy of Engineering, 140 senior scientists and 78 budding scientists. They huddled around a main forum, six parallel forums, four events and one closing ceremony under the umbrella theme "New Science Paradigm: Break Through for the Next Decade." The opening ceremony saw the 2026 World Laureates Foundation (WLF) Prize handed out to 11 scientists for contributions to intelligent science or mathematics, life science or medicine, and a dedicated category for young scientists. Belgian scientist Ingrid Daubechies took home the mathematics award. The life science or medicine award was shared by Yuan Junying, Wang Xiaodong, Shao Feng and Vishva Dixit for clarifying molecular pathways of different forms of programmed cell death. Shao is the first Chinese citizen to win a WLF Prize. Yuan said her greatest wish is to see her lab's findings translated into clinical therapies, calling it the most meaningful reward. Pursuing big ideas needs practical steps. On that note, Wang said trust is essential in scientific collaboration, and a spot of friendly competition has its merits too. Dixit added a philosophical touch, saying people live because cells can die. The gongs were just the start. A question wall let attendees post queries ranging from whether a perfectly smooth ball can spin, to whether consciousness can be read. The future of AI also took center stage. In a keynote address, Fields Medalist Laurent Lafforgue said large language models can already solve some problems human mathematicians have never cracked, but AI cannot shortcut the wisdom that comes from the effort required to actually learn.

items.title: Iran's supreme leader warns US, Israel of 'unrestricted geographical response' to new attacks
items.description: Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Saturday warned the United States and Israel against returning to war, according to a written statement, following threats from the Islamic republic’s foes of a possible resumption of strikes. “If the enemies once again launch military or terrorist attacks, it is the armed forces of the Islamic Republic and the Iranian nation that will determine the time and conditions for ending them,” said a statement attributed to Khamenei posted on his website. The remarks came during a reported meeting between Khamenei and senior military commanders, including armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, army chief Amir Hatami and Revolutionary Guards commander Ahmad Vahidi. It was the first reported meeting between them. Khamenei has not been publicly seen since he became supreme leader, following his father Ayatollah Ali Khamenei’s assassination in US-Israeli strikes at the start of the Middle East war in February. According to the statement, Khamenei ordered the commanders to ensure that “any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response”. It also said that Khamenei ordered the commanders to update Iran’s target list to include “all types of tangible and intangible assets belonging to the American-Zionist (Israeli) enemy”. The war began on February 28 with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, which swiftly responded with attacks on countries around the region. The supreme leader’s statement came as fresh diplomatic efforts were under way to avert a resumption of fighting. A Qatari delegation arrived in Tehran on Friday for talks with Iranian officials, after Iran reportedly received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance. According to Iranian media, Tehran had yet to respond to the letter.

items.title: Mutilations génitales féminines à Labé : Quand la tradition contourne la loi et les campagnes de sensibilisation
items.description: La lutte contre l'excision se heurte à un mur de verre où les discours de prévention semblent prêcher dans le désert à Labé. Traquées par les autorités, les matrones traditionnelles et les familles conservatrices ont troqué les grandes fêtes collectives contre une clandestinité maîtrisée, érigeant la discrétion en bouclier pour préserver la coutume. L’excision se déroule désormais dans la plus stricte discrétion, perpétuant ainsi un rite ancestral perçu comme un passage culturel et social obligatoire, a constaté sur place Guinéenews. A Labé, la capitale de la Moyenne Guinée, le silence qui entoure désormais l'excision est loin d'être le signe de sa disparition. Si les grandes festivités communautaires d'antan se sont tues, la pratique, elle, s'est simplement drapée dans l'ombre, pour mieux perpétuer sa tradition. Face au renforcement de l'arsenal juridique et à la pression constante des acteurs de la société civile, les défenseurs de cette coutume ont préféré adapter leurs stratégies plutôt que d'y renoncer. Des campagnes d'information qui se heurtent au poids des traditions Depuis plusieurs décennies, organisations non gouvernementales, services de santé publique et ministères sociaux, soutenus par les bailleurs de fonds internationaux, multiplient les programmes d'information et d'éducation. L'objectif affiché reste invariable : éradiquer définitivement les MGF. Pourtant, sur le terrain, le constat demeure alarmant. Les discours médicaux et juridiques semblent glisser sur une réalité sociale profondément ancrée. Pour de nombreuses familles, l'excision ne relève pas d'un choix, mais d'une obligation morale et culturelle, transmise de génération en génération. Madame Maladho Barry, ménagère à Labé, résume cette conviction sans détour : « Même si de rares complications surviennent parfois, l’excision reste une étape incontournable. L’ayant subie moi-même, il est évident que mes filles suivront le même chemin. » Cette perception d'un « passage obligé » est renforcée par une forte pression sociale. Dans l’esprit collectif, le rejet du rite expose la jeune fille au mépris et à l'exclusion. « On ne peut pas évaluer la honte qu'éprouve une fille si ses amies apprennent qu’elle n’a pas été excisée. Ici, nous faisons tout pour préserver la dignité de nos familles », renchérit Madame Barry. La stratégie de la clandestinité pour braver la loi Face aux menaces de poursuites judiciaires brandies par l'État, les traditionalistes ont opéré une mutation radicale dans l'organisation de l'acte. Les cérémonies collectives et festives d'autrefois ont laissé place à une pratique clandestine et individualisée. Les parents opèrent désormais dans la plus grande confidentialité, évitant tout rassemblement susceptible de donner l'alerte aux autorités. Le statut culturel accordé au rite demeure un verrou majeur. Pour Mody Amadou Kaba, un sage, respecté de la sous-préfecture de Popodara, supprimer la coutume est tout simplement inconcevable : « Bannir l’excision reviendrait à interdire le mariage religieux pour ne conserver que la cérémonie civile. C’est inacceptable, car il s'agit de notre identité traditionnelle. » Un changement de méthode pour mieux dissimuler l’acte Outre l'individualisation des opérations, les matrones traditionnelles ont ajusté leurs techniques opératoires pour minimiser les indices extérieurs. Une exciseuse opérant sous le couvert de l'anonymat témoigne de cette évolution : « Nous évitons désormais d'élargir la blessure et nous pratiquons l'opération de façon plus moderne. Personne ne s'en rend compte, mais cela suffit à rassurer et réconforter les familles qui le demandent. En quelques jours seulement, la plaie est cicatrisée. » Ce passage à la clandestinité pose un véritable défi stratégique aux ONG et aux autorités. En devenant invisible, le phénomène échappe aux mécanismes classiques de contrôle et de prévention, démontrant la capacité de résistance des structures sociales traditionnelles, face aux interventions extérieures. L'évaluation des programmes de lutte contre l'excision dans la région de Labé révèle une fracture béante entre le cadre légal/sanitaire et les réalités socioculturelles de la communauté. Loin d'avoir éradiqué la pratique, les décennies de sensibilisation ont principalement poussé l'excision vers une clandestinité plus stricte et une méthode plus discrète. Face à ce constat « d'échec » des approches classiques, les acteurs institutionnels et sanitaires n'auront d'autre choix que d'inventer de nouveaux leviers de dialogue avec les garants de la tradition s'ils veulent briser définitivement ce mur du silence.

items.title: Syria weighing whether to join Makkah pact: foreign minister
items.description: Syria’s Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani on Saturday said Damascus was considering whether to join the Makkah defence pact that binds Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye. The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, signed on Aug 7, empowers the three members to consider an armed attack on one member an attack on all. “Discussions are currently underway to evaluate Syria’s entry into the Makkah alliance,” Al Shaibani said at the Manama Dialogue conference in Bahrain. According to Syrian Arab News Agency ( SANA ), speaking about the ongoing regional conflicts, the foreign minister expressed Damascus’s support for the Gulf states against any aggression and condemned missile and drone attacks. “Geography is destiny, and integration is a choice. We have chosen to make our territory a bridge for prosperity and the exchange of interests, and we stand as a bulwark against turning Syria into a platform for threatening neighbouring countries,” he was quoted as saying. Al Shaibani also condemned repeated Israeli attacks on Syrian territory, affirmed that occupied Golan was Syrian land, and called for a path to an independent Palestinian state. Saudi Arabia has been rallying support against escalating attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, including a deadly strike that closed Riyadh’s international airport for two weeks this month. Islamabad has two defence pacts with Riyadh aimed at collective deterrence — the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement between the two and the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement that also includes Turkiye. Pakistan is providing “whatever support is needed” to defend Saudi Arabia amid the Houthi attacks, the military’s spokesperson Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said earlier this month. However, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) director general also clarified that all members of the Makkah Defence Alliance were “absolutely clear […] that this alliance has no offensive intent; it is purely defensive”. A day earlier, he said that the wording of the pact did not bar new members after being asked about whether Iran could join the agreement. “Anyone who has a shared vision of collective deterrence and regional peace, why not? Everyone is most welcome,” he said, adding that it was for the political leadership of the three principal parties to decide. In August, two weeks after the Makkah pact was signed, the Syrian foreign minister visited Pakistan and called on Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir. They both discussed “regional security environment and avenues for enhanced bilateral defence and security cooperation”, ISPR said. Amid the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, French President Emmanuel Macron made a surprise visit to Riyadh earlier this month and said France had sent troops to help shield a key Saudi oil terminal from attacks. Also in October, the United Kingdom’s government announced it would deploy British fighter planes to help Saudi Arabia against the attacks.

items.title: Why Halloween Isn’t Just for Kids
items.description: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight. Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning. Children rarely need an excuse to be silly. They invent games, dress up on a random Tuesday, and find endless amusement in things that might seem mundane to grown-ups. But somewhere along the way, that kind of uninhibited fun becomes harder to come by. Free time for adults is often filled with plans and obligations, and even leisure can start to feel like something we ought to be doing productively. Halloween offers a welcome exception. For one night, adults can put on ridiculous costumes, eat too much candy, and lean into the absurdity. In a 2022 essay for The Atlantic , Faith Hill argued that the holiday’s childishness is precisely what makes it so valuable to grown-ups. Although traditions have changed over time—widespread mischief and juvenile pranks have largely mellowed out, supplanted by trick-or-treating and bar crawls—what remains central to the night’s celebration is the freeing sense that you can do something simply for the pleasure of it, even if that means looking a little silly. Adult Halloween Is Stupid, Embarrassing, and Very Important By Faith Hill The most inherently childish holiday might be the one grown-ups need the most. ( From 2022 ) Read the article. Trick-or-Treating Isn’t What It Used to Be By Julie Beck Instead of going door-to-door on Halloween night, many parents are taking their kids elsewhere to get candy. ( From 2018 ) Read the article. The Costume I Can’t Persuade My Husband to Throw Away By Serena Dai Its name is Wolf Dawg, and it hasn’t been cleaned in 18 years. Read the article. Still Curious? Just noting that your candy corn is made of bug secretions : Tove Danovich regrets to inform you about the shellac that coats your treats. The variety bag has ruined Halloween : Corporate consolidation and changing tastes have made kids’ candy hauls boring, Ian Bogost argues. Other Diversions The rise of the sexy-cozy autumn read There are too many apps for that. The pants that define the Cool Millennial Mom PS Courtesy of Dale E. My colleague Isabel Fattal recently asked readers to share a photo of something that sparks their sense of awe in the world. “After last week’s thunderstorms on Friday, the deep-red maple background behind the wilting morning glories and their green vines captured that moment of transition between vanishing summer and undeniable autumn. Pictures never capture the experience as well as the moment itself, but I am glad I have a record of the color,” Dale E. from Honesdale, Pennsylvania, shared. We’ll continue to feature your responses in the coming weeks. — Rafaela

items.title: He Was Hugely Influential. He Also Had a Foolish Streak.
items.description: I n his memoirs, Giacomo Casanova, the 18th-century writer and libertine, made a helpful distinction between “stupid” people and “fools.” Those who are stupid, he opined, were generally honest and merely lacking in education: “They are like eyes that, if not for their cataracts, would be very beautiful.” Fools, however, he couldn’t abide. He found them conceited and insolent. Worst of all, he wrote, “I feel like a fool whenever I find myself in their company.” We are all, I take Casanova to be saying, stupid to some degree. But it takes a special kind of obliviousness to be a fool. The novelist and art critic John Berger was neither insolent nor conceited, and he was less stupid than most of us. But he undoubtedly had a foolish streak. Berger would have turned 100 this year. He is the subject of a new biography, John Berger: From Life , by Tom Overton, an archive curator at the Barbican Centre, in London, and nearly a decade after his death, at age 90, many of his books are being reissued. Berger was an experimentalist. Apart from his art criticism and fiction, he wrote screenplays, painted, and drew. But he is best known for Ways of Seeing , a 1972 TV series about art and power that is still a staple of art education more than 50 years after it was first aired on the BBC. To rewatch Ways of Seeing , which consists of four 30-minute episodes, is to realize how immensely influential it has been. Like a brilliant college lecturer, Berger methodically builds arguments around four themes: the effects of reproduction on original artworks; art’s role in the objectification of women; the part art has played in establishing social status and ownership; and the reality-distorting role of modern advertising. Berger gets his points across with almost electrifying immediacy. When he presents directly to the camera, you can feel his magnetism instantly. His flaring eyes, mobile brow, and slight difficulty pronouncing the r sound convey his intelligence and moral seriousness with almost comical exaggeration. But Berger’s particular species of charisma was inseparable from his earnestness, which had a relentless quality. Behind it lurked a sort of wet-eyed, slightly indiscriminate craving for human connection. Berger created Ways of Seeing with the producer and director Mike Dibb. A subsequent book , adapted from the series, was a collaboration credited to Berger and four others. The series was interpreted by some as a rebuke to Civilisation , a 13-part documentary from 1969 about European visual culture that was commissioned for the BBC by David Attenborough and presented by Kenneth Clark. But Berger’s early career owed a great deal to Clark, an acclaimed art historian who had been the director of London’s National Gallery, and his shorter TV series was a different project with a narrower aim. [ Read: The seminal TV series that changed how we see ] The title was very much to the point. As if in emulation of his father, who tended to soldiers with damaged eyesight during World War I, he saw himself as removing cataracts from people’s eyes. Berger wrote from a position of principled belief and always from the heart. He was a Marxist who wanted to rescue people from their naivete about the workings of capitalism. In the introduction to Permanent Red , his first collection of essays, he was forthright about his criteria for judging art: “The question I ask is: Does this work help or encourage men to know and claim their social rights?” It’s this quality of yearning—for love, for justice, for compassion—that is still the main reason to read Berger. In his essays and reviews, something deeper than aesthetic judgment always feels at stake. But when you compare his art writing with that of his sharper, less sentimental contemporaries—Susan Sontag, Robert Hughes, Peter Schjeldahl, Janet Malcolm—you’re reminded of Berger’s tendency to belabor the obvious. A plodding, pedagogical flavor compromises much of his criticism (“to return now to our original question”), as if he worried that too much humor or writerly flair might nibble away at his class credentials. Berger understood that images play a huge role in projecting the influence of capital and making wealth enviable. Ways of Seeing demonstrated this in its four pithy episodes. It was an effort to awaken the public to the ways in which injustice was embedded in both the art in our museums and the imagery disseminated across Western culture. Berger derived his insights not only from Karl Marx but also from Marxist thinkers in the 20th century, including his friend Frederick Antal, the pioneering Hungarian art historian who wrote about the social background of Florentine art during the Renaissance; Georg Lukács, the Leninist literary critic and philosopher; and Walter Benjamin, the great media theorist and cultural critic. But Berger’s 1970s-style “consciousness-raising” was aimed at a broad public and proved very successful. Even now, when his critiques have become platitudes, to hear him speak about the male gaze or the depredations of advertising is to feel these notions reinfused with amplitude and urgency. Ways of Seeing catapulted the show’s presenter to fame. That fame turned to notoriety later in 1972, when Berger’s experimental novel G. —about a Casanova-like character caught up in political events around the turn of the 20th century—won the Booker Prize. The book, which Berger spent five years writing, is dedicated to his partner Anya Bostock, an acclaimed translator, and to “her sisters in Women’s Liberation.” This was painful—for Bostock, anyway—because while writing it, Berger had begun an affair with another woman, Annar Cassam. Bostock believed that G. , with its libertine hero, was partly Berger’s attempt to use fiction to understand his own behavior. ( G. might be better recalled today for Berger’s Booker Prize–acceptance speech, in which he criticized the company behind the prize for historically profiting from enslaved labor in the Caribbean; his protest was an attempt, he said, to “turn this prize against itself.”) Overton’s biography provides a useful critical overview of Berger’s writing, as well as of his work for television and radio. Its author, who became close friends with Berger when he cataloged the latter’s archive for the British Library, refers to his subject throughout as “John.” But intermittently, Overton switches to “you,” addressing Berger as if he were still alive and might be able to account for himself. The habit kicks in when Overton is most dismayed by what he has learned about Berger’s unfeeling treatment of his various lovers or of his son Jacob, who made a film that drew on Berger’s life—just as Berger had often used others’ lives in his writing—resulting in a rift that lasted years. Overton’s use of direct address appears to be his way of enacting the special difficulty he faces as Berger’s biographer, effectively letting us listen in as he asks, What do I owe to my subject, who was my friend but is now dead? The question of what we owe the dead obsessed Berger. His preoccupation had its roots in his father’s experiences during World War I. In the wake of that catastrophe, the British fixated on memorializing the dead. Monuments were erected in nearly every village square. Born in 1926, Berger came to believe that humans live along two axes: the horizontal line, which relates to one’s physical place in the world, and the vertical line of time, which connects the living with the dead and those yet to be born. His understanding of the importance of place fed into his writing about migrants displaced by war and the movements of capital. But for Berger, that relationship between the living and the dead was, “almost as soon as he began to think about it, the very core of politics.” “The one question of his work,” Overton believes, “was: how do we live with the dead?” James Fitton, Ruskin Spear, John Berger and John Minton in 1950 (Frank Lilley / Hulton Archive / Getty) The question is obviously profound. It goes to the core of how most cultures have seen and organized themselves. And yet in Berger’s hands, it betrays a proclivity for nostalgia that can be a weakness. To feel too much solidarity with the dead, after all, might be one way to avoid one’s responsibility to the proximate living. M ost things that Berger wrote were connected to art in one way or another. His first novel, A Painter of Our Time , centers on two characters who bond over a painting by Goya in the National Gallery. By the time it was published, in 1958, Berger was ending his second marriage and in the throes of a long romantic relationship with Bostock. He’d begun that decade discussing pictures in the National Gallery for the BBC West African Service and soon started writing exhibition reviews and essays for a variety of publications. Permanent Red appeared in 1960. In 1962, Berger left Britain to begin more than a decade of mobile living from a base in Geneva, where Bostock worked as a translator for the United Nations. This roiling period, personally and politically, came to an end in the early 1970s, soon after Ways of Seeing and G. were released, when he settled in the village of Quincy in the French Pyrenees. Three captivating books, known as the Into Their Labours trilogy, emerged from this period. The first of them, Pig Earth , consists of stories alternating with poems. The trilogy shows Berger at his best: direct, visceral descriptions of real things; a frank engagement with death, birth, and sex; and an acute sensitivity to the rhythms of others’ lives. Even as Berger, like any good Marxist, longed for revolution and promoted solidarity, he was a traditionalist at heart. In art, he liked realism and distrusted abstraction, all the more so as he learned about the CIA’s involvement in promoting abstract expressionism as a form of Cold War soft power. In the 1950s, he had championed the so-called kitchen-sink school of British realists, who have since been largely forgotten. He failed to see merit in the work of more powerful painters, such as Francis Bacon and Lucian Freud, perhaps because their existentialist, amoral worldviews didn’t align with his own brand of progressive humanism. [ Read: The conundrum of Lucian Freud’s portraits ] Overton puts a nice but unconvincing spin on Berger’s blind spots, writing, “John’s focus on deep time, on the necessity of the company of the past, could obscure his view of the contemporary.” For an art critic, that feels like a problem. Berger adored Stanley Spencer (“by far and away one of the most important English artists of our time”) and was impressed by the art he saw on a 1953 visit to Moscow, co-organized by the Communist Party of Great Britain and the Union of Soviet Architects. “I believe that they are creating the foundations of a true tradition,” he wrote, “whereas we, for the most part, are destroying the tradition we inherited.” Berger’s career as an art critic is a reminder that, although certain kinds of naivete deserve to be indulged because they are aligned with compassion, other kinds can become exasperating. Despite mounting evidence of Joseph Stalin’s brutality and the disaster of totalitarianism, Berger, like many Marxists in the West, continued to romanticize the Soviet Union, visiting for a second and third time in 1961 and 1966. “In the early 1950’s,” he explained in a 1979 preface to a reissue of Permanent Red , “the USSR represented, despite all its deformations, a great part of the force of the socialist challenge to capitalism.” Berger’s next sentence—“It no longer does”—was welcome. But his later responses to the fall of the Berlin Wall and the collapse of the Soviet Union were grudging and mealymouthed. Reading them, I found it impossible not to feel that Berger wore ideological blinkers that limited his compassion for the millions who had suffered under the Soviet empire, including countless fellow writers and artists. A similar blinkeredness seemed to drive Berger’s response to the fatwa against the author Salman Rushdie. When Iran’s Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini called for Rushdie’s murder after the publication of The Satanic Verses , Berger took the side of the leader of a theocratic, deeply misogynistic state against a fellow Booker Prize–winning author, who now lived in fear for his life. Berger, in an essay, praised the Quran—Overton notes that, at the time, Berger more and more “thought the real hope of resisting the American world order might lie with Islam”—and dismissed Rushdie’s book, whose portrayal of the Prophet Muhammad had prompted backlash, as “a rather arrogant fiction about playing at being God.” Pitting the two books against each other, Berger noted, “The first is a book about responsibility, the second is a story about irresponsibility.” [ Read: Salman Rushdie strikes back ] The writer Christopher Hitchens, a friend of Rushdie’s, observed at the time, “There has long been a Berger scale for fatuity, but that piece, even in the judgment of seasoned seismographers, went clear off the graph.” Berger felt that he was showing sympathy for those who were hurt by Rushdie’s novel—although how many of them had actually read the book is unclear. But Berger was naive about the motivations behind the fatwa. (It was issued at a moment when Iran was in a power struggle with Saudi Arabia for dominance in the Muslim world and was seeking to project strength; the ayatollah issued the fatwa only after a part of the book, which includes a character who appears to caricature Khomeini, was read aloud to him.) Berger should have condemned, without hedging, the inhumanity of the autocratic regime that was calling for a fellow writer’s death. “I do not expect many to listen to arguments like mine,” he concluded in his essay, with the maudlin tone that colors too much of his writing. “The colonial prejudices are still too ingrained.” Berger’s writing, at its strongest, has a quality of thinking in process that can be immensely engaging. His essays “are all the time testing his life, probing and assessing it,” Geoff Dyer wrote in his introduction to Berger’s Selected Essays . But being exposed to too much of the clanking machinery of thought, especially for a reader not convinced by its premises, can become wearying. Overton rightly points out that Berger did not have a talent for storytelling: “He had no ear for rhythm, or gift for narrative.” Instead, he was at his best a “conduit for the lives of others,” and his unique skill was to “use paintings, drawings, photographs to drill holes in time, to make channels to the future as much as to the past.” I think Berger appeals especially to people who revel in the romance of failure—failed ideals and conceptions of the world. He loved Stendhal, the great Romantic-era writer who survived Napoleon’s disastrous retreat from Moscow. He wanted to think of himself as “a kind of marxist Stendhal.” But Tony Godwin, Berger’s book editor, sensed the danger in his author’s Romantic inclinations. He tried to remind him that his job was to supply “the vision, the insight and the reminder of humanity.” “You’re not a political commentator,” he warned Berger. “You’re an artist, and it is your duty to guard yourself from fragmenting your time, especially in journalism.” This was surely Godwin’s polite way of saying: Don’t make a fool of yourself—or of me .

items.title: Pakistan’s Punjab records 4.2 times more crop-fire detections than Indian Punjab: report
items.description: LAHORE: Crop-fire detections in Pakistan’s Punjab were 4.2 times higher than in Indian Punjab during the first 29 days of October, according to satellite data, as the province grapples with worsening smog. According to an analysis published by environmental monitoring website HamariHawa , Nasa satellites detected 13,241 fire spots in Pakistan’s Punjab between Oct 1 and 29, compared with 3,158 in Indian Punjab — 4.2 times as many detections. The report, based on data from Nasa’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), collected through VIIRS instruments aboard the Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 satellites, found that 92 per cent of the detected fire spots in Pakistan’s Punjab were located on farmland and were likely associated with crop burning. The analysis also found that 6,655 fire spots, around half of the monthly total, were detected during the last seven days of October, indicating an increase in burning activity. Oct 29 was the busiest day, with 1,327 fire spots recorded in Pakistan’s Punjab. A comparison based solely on data from the Suomi NPP satellite, which provides a consistent basis for examining trends over different years, showed that 4,562 fire spots were detected in Pakistan’s Punjab, compared with 918 in Indian Punjab, between Oct 1 and 29. The findings mark a reversal of the situation in 2019, when Indian Punjab recorded almost five times as many fire detections as Pakistan’s Punjab during the same period, with 14,002 compared with 2,908. HamariHawa ’s historical analysis showed that Indian Punjab reduced its satellite-detected crop fires by 95 per cent between 2021 and 2025, while detections in Pakistan’s Punjab increased by 33 per cent between 2019 and 2025. In 2025, Pakistan’s Punjab recorded 12,364 fire spots, compared with 3,714 in Indian Punjab — 3.3 times as many. The latest data showed that agricultural burning in Pakistan’s Punjab was concentrated in the rice-growing belt around Lahore. Okara recorded the highest number of fire spots, at 2,144, followed by Gujranwala with 1,011 and Nankana Sahib with 1,003 between Oct 1 and 29. Graphic showing concentration of fires detected during the month of October — HamariHawa The three districts collectively recorded 4,158 fire spots, exceeding the total of 3,158 detections recorded across Indian Punjab during the same period. Pakpattan recorded 922 fire spots, followed by Sheikhupura with 756, Hafizabad with 713, Dera Ghazi Khan with 710, Kasur with 699, Khanewal with 682 and Jhang with 676. The report noted that these districts lie around Lahore, meaning smoke from agricultural fires across different parts of the province could contribute to the city’s deteriorating air quality, depending on wind direction. However, the website cautioned that satellite detections indicate locations where fires were burning when satellites passed overhead and do not measure the area burnt or the volume of smoke produced. Fires occurring between satellite passes, or those obscured by clouds and thick smoke, may also go undetected. HamariHawa said it had used the same methodology on both sides of the border and cross-checked its figures for Indian Punjab against official Indian fire counts, finding a strong correlation between the two datasets. It also pointed out that Pakistan had no comparable publicly available official daily fire-count series. The satellite findings come as the Punjab Environment Protection Agency (EPA) intensifies its pre-smog enforcement campaign across the province, combining action against brick kilns, industrial pollution, plastic burning and construction dust with measures to prevent agricultural fires. According to official figures for Sept 28 to Oct 27, the agency inspected 11,580 brick kilns, demolished 197 non-compliant kilns, sealed 163 units and registered 162 cases. Fines amounting to Rs40.7 million were also imposed during the operation. Industrial pollution was another target, with 6,650 industrial units inspected, 22 demolished and 191 sealed. Officials issued 333 smog notices, registered 15 cases and imposed fines totalling Rs28m. The agency also conducted 6,064 inspections targeting plastic burning, sealed 152 sites and confiscated 45,100 kilogrammes of plastic. In a separate exercise to monitor the installation of suction hoods at industrial facilities, 4,204 units were inspected, of which 1,863 had installed the required equipment. A total of 333 non-compliant sites were sealed. To control dust from construction activities, operations were conducted in 397 union councils, with mist sprinklers installed at 49 locations. In agricultural areas, the Punjab government has deployed 67 Quick Response Units (QRUs) to identify and prevent crop-residue burning through satellite-based fire detection and field monitoring. The teams are tasked with reaching fire hotspots, extinguishing fires and taking action against those responsible. The department has also deployed drones, special night squads and field teams to identify pollution sources and enforce environmental regulations. Anti-smog guns are being operated at selected locations across Lahore to suppress suspended dust particles. Meanwhile, according to the live air quality ranking published by Swiss air quality monitoring platform IQAir, Lahore recorded an Air Quality Index (AQI) of 232 at 1pm on Oct 31, placing it at the top of the list of the world’s major cities. The readings placed Lahore in the ‘very unhealthy’ category. Figure shows the top ranked polluted cities according to IQAir on Saturday afternoon. — Screengrab via IQAir Director General Environment Abdullah Nayyar Sheikh said the department was implementing a zero-tolerance policy against pollution, with enforcement teams remaining active during the day and at night. He said action through fines, registration of cases and sealing of premises would continue against those violating environmental laws. The satellite findings, meanwhile, highlight the challenge of controlling agricultural fires, particularly in districts surrounding Lahore, as the province enters the period when crop-residue burning and other pollution sources can combine to aggravate winter smog.

items.title: Tunis | Peine de mort pour le meurtrier d’une fillette de 5 ans
items.description: La chambre criminelle du Tribunal de première instance de Tunis a condamné à la peine de mort par pendaison un jeune homme accusé d’avoir assassiné la fille de ses voisins, âgée de cinq ans, dans le quartier d’El Omrane El Aala, à la lisière nord-ouest de Tunis. L’accusé a étranglé l’enfant avant de dissimuler son corps sur le toit de la maison d’un voisin, après l’avoir enveloppé dans le tissu d’un rideau. Les faits remontent au 2 mai 2025, pendant le mois de Ramadan. Une famille résidant à El Omrane El Aala a constaté la disparition de sa fille — âgée d'un peu plus de cinq ans — avant que son corps ne soit découvert sur le toit de la maison d’un voisin, enveloppé dans le tissu d’un rideau. L’enquête a mené à un jeune voisin qui s’était réfugié chez une connaissance dans le quartier d’Ettadhamen. Le suspect, surnommé «Ruby» et qui vivait seul avec sa mère, avait l’habitude de fréquenter les jeunes enfants du voisinage. Il a avoué que la victime s’était rendue au domicile de sa mère accompagnée de son frère cadet pour y récupérer des écouteurs. Revenue plus tard, seule cette fois, il l’a alors étranglée par-derrière à l’aide d’une chaussette, jusqu’à ce qu’elle ait cessé de respirer. Il a ensuite enveloppé son corps dans le tissu d’un rideau, puis l’a transporté hors de la maison. S’assurant que les lieux étaient déserts, il est monté sur le toit de la maison d’un voisin pour y dissimuler le corps qui n’a pas tardé à être découvert, ce qui a conduit à son arrestation et à ses aveux, rapporte le site Babnet . I. B. L’article Tunis | Peine de mort pour le meurtrier d’une fillette de 5 ans est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Mobilisation JOJ : Le Président Diomaye Faye imprime une innovation dans sa communication
items.description: À la veille de l’ouverture des Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse (JOJ) Dakar 2026, le président de la République, Bassirou Diomaye Faye a choisi de s’adresser aux Sénégalais autrement. Pas de pupitre, pas de décor institutionnel, encore moins de protocole apparent. Un téléphone, une caméra frontale, le drapeau du Sénégal en arrière-plan et un message adressé directement à ses compatriotes. En quelques secondes, le chef de l’État a déplacé le centre de gravité de sa communication. Cette vidéo selfie rompt avec une certaine approche de la parole présidentielle, généralement construite autour de la solennité, de la mise en scène institutionnelle et d’une certaine distance. Ici, le Président parle à hauteur de citoyen, dans un format familier aux usages quotidiens des réseaux sociaux. Son message emprunte à la spontanéité des plateformes numériques, où la proximité compte parfois autant que le contenu. La parole officielle se fait conversationnelle, le cérémonial s’efface au profit d’une adresse directe. Ce choix répond aussi à la nature particulière de l’événement. Les JOJ ne sont pas uniquement une compétition sportive. Ils constituent un rendez-vous de portée internationale dont la réussite dépend également de l’adhésion populaire. En appelant directement les Sénégalais, le Président veut faire de la mobilisation citoyenne une composante à part entière de l’événement. O.BA

items.title: Sahara occidental : à l’ONU, l’Algérie fait le parallèle avec la Palestine
items.description: En utilisant son droit de veto contre la résolution américaine visant à modifier le mandat de la Minurso vendredi 30 octobre, la Russie a sauvé la légalité internationale dans le dossier du Sahara occidental . L'Algérie, par la voix de son représentant à l’ONU, Amar Bendjama, a remercié la Russie pour avoir présenté un projet de reconduite du mandat de la mission ainsi que tous les pays membres qui ont choisi « de ne pas s’associer à une injustice et une atteinte manifeste aux fondements » de l’organisation onusienne. L’Algérie a demandé à participer à la réunion du Conseil en sa qualité de pays voisin, de pays hôte de centaines de milliers de réfugiés sahraouis et d’État membre de l’ONU, « attaché à la légalité internationale et au respect des buts et principes de la Charte des Nations Unies », a expliqué le diplomate algérien dans son intervention dans laquelle il a décortiqué le dossier en six « mots-clés ». Amar Bendjama : « Qui a peur de la démocratie ? » S’adressant aux États-Unis, « pen holder » du dossier, Amar Bendjama a rappelé qu'« être porte-plume est une lourde responsabilité », et « un devoir moral de mériter la confiance des parties, de susciter leur adhésion, par une attitude attentive, impartiale et équitable ». « Ces critères ont-ils été appliqués dans la rédaction du texte qui vous a été soumis aujourd’hui ? Je vous laisse méditer la réponse », a-t-il dit. Évoquant l’autodétermination, qui a « depuis toujours constitué une référence fondamentale pour le règlement du conflit » et qui est « la forme la plus évidente, la plus sûre et la plus incontestable pour le libre exercice par un peuple du choix de son propre avenir », Bendjama s'est demandé « qui a peur de la démocratie » au point de vouloir cantonner l’autodétermination « à l’intérieur d’un statut d’autonomie dont la plupart d’entre vous ne connaissent que le titre, même si vous l’avez cautionné ». La négociation, ce n'est pas « imposer une conclusion prédéterminée » Le représentant de l’Algérie s'est aussi attardé sur l’expression « solution politique mutuellement acceptable ». « La négociation est un cheminement qui demande écoute attentive des protagonistes, patience, et innovation avec pour objectif une solution acceptable par tous, pour tous », a-t-il rappelé. Or, ni les propositions du Front Polisario ni les préoccupations et réserves faites « candidement » par les deux pays voisins, l’Algérie et la Mauritanie n'ont été « entretenues », a-t-il déploré, dénonçant un texte qui considère « ces négociations comme étant achevées, et ce, avant même qu’elles n’aient commencé ». « La négociation doit être un cheminement vers une solution, et non un moyen d’imposer une conclusion prédéterminée », a asséné Bendjama. Quant à la souveraineté, qui est « une des normes contraignantes du droit international », « nul n’a le droit de conférer à une puissance occupante une propriété qu’il ne possède pas de jure », a-t-il soutenu, regrettant l’altération de cette norme qui « ouvre la porte à toutes les aventures, à l’imposition de la volonté du plus fort sur le plus faible ». Un « fait accompli » résultat d’une « transaction indécente » Le cinquième mot-clé du dossier, selon Amar Bendjama, est le « fait-accompli » de l’invasion et l’annexion d’un territoire non autonome que la résolution américaine veut légaliser. « Ce fait accompli est le résultat d’une transaction indécente conclue aux dépens du peuple palestinien, un peuple qui a tant souffert. Et maintenant, c’est au peuple sahraoui que l’on demande de payer de sa propre liberté les dividendes promis comme rétribution à l’occupant », a-t-il dénoncé, en allusion aux accords de normalisation Maroc-Israël en échange de la reconnaissance par les États-Unis de la « souveraineté marocaine » sur le Sahara occidental. « Humanitaire » : triple peine pour les réfugiés sahraouis Évoquant enfin l’« humanitaire », le représentant de l’Algérie à l’ONU a signifié que les réfugiés sahraouis « sont des êtres humains, pas de simples chiffres ». L’initiative, « dont on veut embarquer le HCR », est synonyme d’une « triple peine » pour les réfugiés sahraouis, a mis en garde Bendjama. Il s’agit, a-t-il expliqué, de « la perpétuation de leur souffrance dans le désert du Sahara », d’un « chantage à la famine qui est actuellement en cours, par la réduction drastique des rations alimentaires à une population déjà affectée par un taux alarmant de malnutrition » et d’un « déplacement forcé, proposé comme alternative et solution durable ». En conclusion, Amar Bendjama a assuré que l’Algérie, qui a exercé son droit à l’autodétermination « au prix de lourds sacrifices », continuera « de manière sincère et déterminée à promouvoir une solution juste, durable et mutuellement acceptable qui garantit le droit du peuple sahraoui à l’autodétermination ». L’article Sahara occidental : à l'ONU, l'Algérie fait le parallèle avec la Palestine est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: UK PM 'open' to slavery apology but not reparations
items.description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Saturday he was “open” to the UK issuing a formal apology for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, but ruled out financial reparations. The Labour leader made the remarks days before attending a Commonwealth leaders summit in Antigua and Barbuda, as King Charles III tours the Caribbean. “I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today,” Burnam wrote in The Guardian newspaper. The transatlantic slave trade was a “brutal and barbaric violation” of the rights of those enslaved, he said, adding that his government wanted a “structured dialogue with those affected”. “Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process, and I am open to them.” The king is due to address the Commonwealth summit, which runs from November 1 to 4. Britain’s central role in slavery and the treatment of people in its former colonies has loomed over the 77-year-old monarch’s Caribbean tour. In the Bahamas on Tuesday, Charles acknowledged “the great suffering of the past” during the first leg of his visit. The UK has never formally apologised for slavery nor or agreed to pay reparations. Burnham again rejected financial compensation, writing: “I do not believe that is the right answer. “I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.” Britain profited for centuries from colonialism and the slave trade. In 1833, parliament passed a law to abolish slavery.
